div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

UT DEAR NELLIE. There has been no particular change in the style of ball dresses since I last addressed you. Whey continue to afford the dressmaker plenty of !employment, there being such a nuniber of them which tend to show up the fact that everybody who feels called upon to wear them, at least pur- !chases one for the winter, whilst many people of any acquaintance have several. One of these :showed me her latest garment the ether day, and a must say I like it immensely. The dress was composed of maisseline de sole in a deep pleated flounce. At the shoulders were light puffing of gauze. The bodice was of the tunic mode and in +cream. Falling straight from the shoulders was light gauze material caught at the waist by a silver band and terminating in a long peplum covered with silver embroidery. The only trimming was in the shape of thin trefoil of green velvet, encased , in bows of gauze, which fastened the bodice on the left side. The dress altogether as you may judge looked very youthful and exquisite.

It really zesms a very long time since I had the pleasure of addressing you upon the subject of muffs that you will think they have completely gone out of fashion, or at least out of my memory. It is not so however. Petlelps the recent cold weather brought to ray rind more-forcible than anything else that there were such things in this world as muffs. ney are to be obt.-,ined at nearly every draper and costumier. I paid. a visit to a shop yesterday and purchased such a delightful warm article. The bedy of the muff was ecroneeed of sealskin trimmed with sable and beautiful heavy black ribbon. The interior NM3 lined with red Bilk, and the article taken altogether is giving satisfaction.

A friend of mine I saw recently wearing a very comfortable walking coat. I have no doubt 1 hat she also utilised it when out driving for it looked very warm and comfortable. It was full length, in fact covered the dress completely, and the way it fitted took my fancy completely. You know 1, with a good many more that I could name, inelud- ing yourself, know that I detest a badly-fitted ox badly-made costume of any kind, and when such a thing occurs in long articles the hight looks abso- lutely appalling. The dress was composed of black cloth, which looked of good thickness. It had a heavy fur collar which was surrounded with warm fur of a brownish hue and looked as if it would resist the greatest frost. The front of the dress wos lined with similar coloured fur, which reached right down to the ground. The garment was lined with rich white and black fur, which of course added considerably to the warmth. The wrists were also surrounded with a cuff of fur. There was a pocket on both sides lined with silk, tending to make the coat wholly comfortable.

Now for a little sweetmeat. This is the way to rnake chocolate caramels. Put half a cupful of butter in a saucepan, and when melted add one cupful of sugar, two cupfuls of, treacle, and half a csupful of milk or create. Stir until the sugar is all dissolved, and when the boiling point is I%l3i:ilea, add three squares of grated chocolate. Boil till, when tried in cold water, a fiLeli ball may be formed. Add a teaspoonful of vanilla after taking from the fire. Turn into butter-pans, and when nearly cold, mark it in inch squares, and later wrap in waxed paper. You ask me for a dress for evening wear but riot actually a evening teilette. Hew will this ? A sweet little demi-toilette of caetmere or voile, delicately embroidered on the front of the skirt and side of the bodice with that pretty white lace that NA a black cord run through it. Velvet revers decorated to match, and a wired lace collar standing up at the back. A black chiffon sash drawn through a paste buckle completes the details .of an elegant costume. It could be carried but -effectively in any delicaie eolcur. such as pale-blue, :rose-pink, or Russian violet. The skirt' touches 7the ground at the back, or rather reste on it, and is of the new, soft, ciinl;ing order, and, therefore, !tune:lit of interlining. Unfortunately, I think earrings are coming into fashion again, and I am afraid there is a tendency for them to become universal. Although several of the great writers of the age speak in praise of ,them, it seems to me there is too much a tinge of :barbarism about them. The earrings which I have seen of late have only been of diamonds, worn by those who can afford the real or imitation, but the Americans are trying to bring them in to match the different costumes, which would requisition adiy number of stones. Grey gowns trimmed with blue are accompanied by turquoise earrings, and dark green by malachite. In conclusion, I hope you have spent a Merry Christmas, and are starting with a Happy New Year.
Your loving JENNIE.

The tucks were eighth of an inch depth throughout. Need less to relate the prospective wearer is of slender build and tall, " divinely tall." I might e o further and ~ay that she is divinely fair" too, only that has no bear- ing on the subjectof the moment. Such a mode is cer- tainly for slight figures only. A well-proportioned indi- vidual (one never says stout nowadays) attired in a gown, such as I have described, would be a terrible &e- -ject indeed. Every girl knows how frequently ostrich feathers v- quire recurling, and what expensive items they even- tually prove, if the operation has to be carried out by a cleaner. Now the curling 2an be done perfectly at hcma with a little care and patience. Get a Larrow and sharp ivory, silver,or wooden paper knife—never use anything with a keener edge, or it scrapeel the fluff eff the strands of the feather—take the extreme tip of the plume, and with your thumb on the top, scrape the knife hard along the ued,r part of the rib, to as to curl it. Then curl the undermost strands oa the left side, taking them in bunches of four or five at a time. Do not curl them very tightly, but make them curl over roundly from the entire rib of the plume. When you have done this to both sides, take the upper strands that are left three or four from Each side together at a time, and curl them so as to cover the rib all the way. Then shake your feather in front of a hot fire, when you will find many strands standing up here ani there. These require individual curling, and the whole should be arrangel to look swat and compact.
" MADGE."

div.head: " WOMEN'S CHIT."
div.p: " WOMEN'S CHIT."

The Queen nowadays, rarely reads to herself, but she is read to for several hours each day, and is always a most patient and attentive listener. The newspapers come first, and she Will often have one paragraph read three or four times if the desires to remember it word for word. A good clever novel is mach appreciated by Her Majesty, and so Loon as anything new in this way makes ts appearance, the Maids of Honour in attend- ance are supposed t read the book, and be ready with a report upon it. Should this be deemed a favourable one, by the Sovereign, the volume is commenced, and taken up in spare time. The life of a Maid of Honour during her periods of duty,is by no means an easy one. She must invariably be within call, she is expected to stand always in thel Royal presence, and her voice has to be as tireless as her limbs. The salary of a Maid of Honour was nail recently £3OO a year, but this has now been raised to £4OO. If she marries with her Royal Mistress's consent, she receives a gift of £lOOO. Prince Alexander, and Princess Ena of Rattenberg have been constantly dining with the Queen of late, to their unbounded delight. They are both very sweet children, and Immense favourites with their Royal Grandmother. Princess En a is quite a litde Scotch- woman. She was horn at Balmoral baptized by Dr. Cameron Lees, of Edinburgh, and has alwqa been sur- rounded since her babyhood by Scotch attendants. The little Princess is a bright clever girl, and a capital horsewoman. Since her accident however, when she was thrown from her pony and remained insensible for several hours. mu Cil less freedom has been accorded her in the pursuit of her favourite exercise. "The birth of a New Year" says Charles Lamb, "is of an interest too wide to be pretermitted by king or cob- bler. No one over regarded the first of January with indifference. It is that from which all date their time and count upon what is left. It is the nativity of our c =men Adam." The first day of the year seems to have been celebrated by the most ancient nations as a solemn religious festival. By the Jew, as well as the Mohammedan, by the Chinese, the Roman, and the Eeyptian.it was marked by the observance of particular ceremonies.

Among the old Romans, tbe year, in the earliest times began in March, and it was the secend Kine of Rome who altered it to the let of January. Janus, the god of the month, had two fares, one looking back over the year just closed, one looking forward into the future. It is only in comparatively recent times that an aer?e- ment has been errivcd at, as to when the New Year communes. The Gregorian reform ition of the calendar was e. cepted by catholic countr.es, but it was long re- jected by Protestants. It was adopted by Englaed in 1752, when it was provided that the legal year should commence in future on the lit Jenuary, and not al heretofore, on the 25th of March. The old style how- ever, practically prevails in the accounts of the English Treasury. Christmas dividends are not considered doe till Twerth Day. The first day of the Chancellor of tW. YFOTIL Glove Factories employ tie less than 4,f500 hands. Within the last quarter of a century the borough has grown wocclerfully, and it would to difficult to find a more flourishing or go-shad place. Houses and new streets have sprung up where only yesterday, it seems, were green fields, and one of the meet pleasant parts of the town, Pen Mel, is an almost entirely new district. Ten Teen; ago there was scarcely a house to be seen, hut now it is a regular little city. Victoria-etrect is one of the mest recent additions. Here resides Mr, Kennard, Russell, who is aeout thirty years of age, a earpenter by trade, a prominent member of the Ye )vil Volunteersond a person of reptite, as the local paper has lel ely inter- viewed him. "Hearing he bed an interesting *try to tell," a Yeovil newspaper man writes, "I cailed upon him. No. 2, Victoria-street has a nice plo, of garden eround, and at the time of my visit Mr. Russell was badly engaged in hoeing. A few ehott weeks ago such a task would, to him, lave bean imponible, for ho was than suffering from an acute attack of sciatica, but he had now entirely recovered,as a glauce at his erect figure showed. ; "Yee, I have been bad, very bad," he said,in response to the first query. " I first felt my left leg begin to go: stiff, especially at bedtime, and when at work. It got worse, arid I could hardly do anything." His wife interposed aid infermed the reporter that things grew so serious" Keenard ceuld not sit down to his meals le,cause it hurt him to bend his leg. And," she continued, " I had to suffer a; well as him, for the pain made him so short•tempered, you know." This re- mark raised a smile, in which the pressman joined. But to con:inue the patient's story." One day," he said," I read a little beak which was left at, the house ef a friend of mine, a Mr. Cruse, who used to be a policeman here, but is now in the Metropolitan force He had had sciatica' and had been cured by taking Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and I wondered at the time if they would de me good, and, a; it happened, my wife bought a box of the pll5 unknown to me and brought them home. She told me that as she had bought them I must try them, se I did, and I am yore thankful I did. I used to take two of the pids with me to work each morning, and every day I got better and be:ter, until the pains went right away." "I suppose you took more than one box 2" aelced the

scribe. "No ; I only hid the one box, hut the sciatica is gone, and I'm right glad of it I can tell you." "I suppose your mates were a bit surprised ?" the newspaper man asked. " Well." replied Mr. Buasell. " they laughed at me when I used to take my pills each morning, but I diktat mind because I knew they we,e doing me gocd " " You look well enough now," tke journalist r:- marked. " Yes ; and Ido not fear another attack. Even if it did come, I should I now what to take." a,u- retiree wi- we oenorita at yon shantie" —he pointed with the stem of his pipe towards the Merced Grove—"was stabbed through the heart Nire ti, stiletto ez belonged to ,The Butterfly." "Butterfly ? " reiterated Mark, filling his pipe and sitting carelessly back. "Thet's the nickname we give this fine. fancy lady; by gosh, the smartest an' pootiest woman rve kern across, but wi' a deuce of a temper. Well, ez luck would hey' it, a negress thet done ',he rough work was the first to discover her dead master lyin' in his arm-chair covered wi' blood. IShe screamed, an' everybody went mad with excite- ment. Some time a' ter, in walks The Butterfly, ez innocent-like ez a child. But the ne,gress recog- nised the dagger, an' the guilty party fainted -out- !right. Thar was a reg,'lar scene, but the Spaniard was too cunnin' fer the servants, an' When she kern to herself she swore she'd see'd a kind o' Mexican cavortin' about the valley fer days." "And Was that true ? " Mark asked listlessly, as our host paused to push his lighted tobacco home. "Well, it was proved so far ez this. At noon * to-day .ratz, of our shepherds seed a , gap in the frozen stow coverin' a creek near by, an' on lookin' , down thar was the body of a Mexican knocked about suthin' awful. I'm darned sure it was a !ghastly sight; fer when I was called on to help !carry the body into a shed fer examination, it 'turned me right sick." 1 Is it there now ? " asked Mark carelessly, as he blew away the spiral columns of tobacco smoke. "Yes, in a coffin knocked together by our lads." "Was the Senorita aware of it? "She ordered the coffin."

"Did it affect her very much ? " "Ef it did, she had the cunnin' not to shew it. But the awkward part fer her was thet I had seen the Senorita wi' thet very man about a fortnight ago canoodlin' up the valley, both on' em together." "Have you told anybody about this ? " "Not ez yet," replied mine host in a confidential tone, and leaning towards Mark. 'Then you ought," urged my wily companion with an air of indifference; we owe a duty to society." The Settler took the bait. "Jest you wait a wee till the surgeon ,keins over to view the bodies to- morrow a'ternoon, an' ef I . don't jest let on, I'm gam knocked silly!" "How long has the Senorita been living here with—ah, let me see," callously added Mark, tapping his forehead to indicate a forgetful memory or an absence of interest—" with Mr. What's-his- name ? " • "Well, I calkilate about seven weeks; an' she could twist him round her little finger." Our host twirled his own significantly. "If you suspect a certain party guilty of both murders, what was the motite ? " "Thar I reckon I'm done. But ef izoofs kern along much stronger , to-morrow. .thet pooty Spaniard's neck'll try odds wi' a safe noose an' a pine bough away in the grove." He pointed in the direction, as he stood smoking and warming him- self before the bright stove-lire. "Per, ye Must know, the guv'nor was a jolly sorter kind; tho' I'm hanged ef I ea,n think of his name." "Rich ? " asked my diplomatic friend, knocking out the ashes of his pipe on the stove, and preparing to make a move. Well-to-do. Attended the auction at Yerba Buena when San Leno was in the market, an' bid a high price. Sold to the State at a big profit, an' then kern here. Sorry fer his fancy Butterfly—dam pocty lady; but can't help it.", "Where is this Mark Pepys ? " nay friend care- lessly inquired. • "Swaller'd up in Golden Vale wi' Queen Kana an' her people. He got spliced to Princess Olive." "What has come o' that fellow Miro," I asked —"that weak imitation o' Dick Turpin ? " "Took ship an' gone abroad." Mark rose. "What—not stoppin the night? What's yer hurry? Ye're welcome to a shakedown in the outhouse, or in here, if ye prefer." "No thanks," said my leader kindly. "We have several miles to go before the moon gets up. Much oblig( d for your hospitality." And Mark shook hands. "What a big feller!" exclaimed the settler with a broad grin. "I reckon ye've swelled out. El ye kern along this way agen, jest knock us up; night or day ye're welcome. Ye both look better already." "It is the San Leno brandy," said Mark with a merry twinkle in his eyes. "Haven't tasted a drop for many a day." "Whar bound fer ? " Mark winked at me, unobserved by our host. ‘,ll-, Golden Gate," said my friend uncon- cernedly. "Good-bye."
CHAPTER x7cic. QUID PRO QUO.

-- - We shook hands, beckoned to the Indian, whom we had banished to the outhouse during our con- versation, and the three of us trudged off down the valley while our good-tempered host stood on his threshold, a puzzled look on his face, as though he wondered whether he had entertained angels unawares. . "So the life of The Butterfly will be crushed out to-morrow," Mark muttered;-4' Well, I must be that surgeon, arrived sooner than expected, " and you must play second fiddle as my assistant. It will be the ' Open Sesame' to Lucia's house, with- out in any way alarming the servants. It is an advantage that this redskin is so reticent. He must be posted outside." He looked back, and added : " I see we are out of the settler's view ; let us, by a detour, fetch this house of mourning." We speedily reached the house, and when the old negreas ushered us into a room and then went to announce the surgeon, Lucia came forward with the utmost sang-froid. . "The subterfuge was not necessary," said she. "You see by my manner that I am indifferent. The . truth is, I saw you coining to the house. Be as brief as possible, for you may both sully your ' reputation by being under this roof. What is your business with me? ' Her manner was dignified but callous, and the tone in which she spoke unwarrantably formal. . "We come," said Mark, watching Lucia's pale face, and noticing her shifty look, "to borrow horses and provisions for the remnant of my party, who starve at the foot of the Sierra." "Is the favoured half-caste amongst them? " Lucia quietly asked, toying .with her fan and com- pressing her lips. The colour mounted to Mark's pale cheek as he drew himself up. "My wife anxiously awaits our return. My gratitude can never repay her devotion during the most fearful sufferings that travellers can experience." "Indeed! Then why does she tarry? " This with sa sly lock and a smile. "Because her health will not permit her to travel so far. You see my clothes hang like bags upon me; and Sandy is reduced to a skeleton." "Then why condescend to ask a woman's help? 1 Women have no hearts—women are not constant— 1 women are not fit for Senor Dees to associate with 1 —and I have been the object of his aversion. Oh, ' pray excuse my playfulness," she added cheerfully; "though you have wounded me, yet now I will slim, you thatkven a woman of my temperament can rise above petty spite. Most of us would wish 1-,o begin life over again, so as to start well. But philosophy is not my forte. Have you supped ? " When we both assured her we had, she looked ' out through the passage, softly closed the door, glided about the room to assure herself that there ‘ere no eavesdroppers, and then signed us to be seated. We obeyed with some misgiving. "Through my telescope," she said, "I saw you I come from the cabin of a danc/erons gossip—a man generous but prying. I think there is more misery wrought in 'the world by people who cannot keep their tongues between their teeth than by strong drink. Scandal is the most popular form of gossip; I have lately had my share, and I writhe under it when alone. It is my penance. Doubtless yonder settler has\ told you his Version of my neiv drama, ' Beauty and the Beast' ?" "We have an inkling," averred Mark, at which Lucia's face resembled that of a nun repeating her " Ave Maria, "—"but a mere outline." "H'in! now you wish to spare my feelings; it is very considerate of you." She nervously tapped the floor with her dainty foot, while her white lips were twitching with suppressed concern. "And what knowledge you possess has not deterred you asking my help. That surprises me !" "A7crust at your hands, Senorita, is better than luxury at a.nother's," said Mark in the same strain, and with a slight genuflection. • "A very p:!etty compliment," she returned with a wintry smile. There was an awkward pause, and Lucia again glided to the door to assure herself that nobody listened. Then with a business-like air she added: "Now, if I accede to your request, and give you the ill-gotten gold and kind belonging to the Brute, and you reach Olive safely, what are your future plans? " Mark hesitated, his face puzzled. Lucia broke the silence. , "I pardon your reticence, for within you con- Iflicting interests war for the mastery. You fear to be candiii, owing to my apparent deception." Mark
Knocitea rug toe with the hanuie or his whip anti cast his eyes downward. "My words and my actions appear irreconcilable. Of course, it is awkward, but surely when a man is in_desperata
straits tie cannot afford to quibble. You grant
that ? "

_ "Certainly," he answered deliberately, the while I keenly noted the expression on Lucia's face, of which she appeared conscious. "Then apart altogether from that chivalry due to my sex, your own good judgment will dictate your course of action." She rang a bell. "I will shew you both bodies, as an evidencce of my good faith this time 1" This was uttered with tragic firmness, and I began to think Lucia was half crazy. The entrance of the negress, however, revealed the command which the Senorita had over her feelings, for

although the coloured woman was dreadfully flurried, her mistress was surprisingly calm and queenly. "Bring me a lighted lantern, Sarah; this tall gentleman is Dr. -, and the shorter one his assistant." The surname mentioned belonged to one of the oldest families of the British nobility, which, for obvious reasons, I forbear publishing to the world. At the mention of this family name Mark started like one aghast. Lucia's cynical smile and attitude of feigned surprise shewed me that she knew the secret why he left England, and why Harry Puke said he would not care, to return. This woman was smartcr than I bargained for. The negress curtseyed and retired. Meanwhile Lucia busied herself with lighting a couple of _ _ _ _

candles. I glanced at Mark's- face-, and if was a study; a study of strength under the spell of witch- craft, for this woman's power appeared super- natural. And yet this delusion of mine was imme- diately dispelled, for when she turned and beheld his countenance she advanced very quietly, and, nodding sideways at me, said: "Your Secret is safe in our hands. I know; your friend is to be trusted. The crude design branded
on your cattle corresponds with the tattoo on you! arm."

"You are dreaming, Lucia. You mistake me fox some other man. I have no tattoo on my arm.' He pulled up his sleeves with alacrity. • "Indeed! Then you have successfully obliteratetl it. See, there is the red patch! You have pricked
out the device of your 'college at Oxford, from which place you fled for much the same reason that started Muro on his wild career ! " _ _
"How came you to know this?" asked Mark in a hushed voice. _ _
"The Brute • rolled and swept the cricket-field when yt)11. were what he termed a fag' at Winchester school. He was a bully and a hanger-

on at Oxford when you were w there. COrne in,,, she added, in answer to a knock, "Thank you, Sarah; put the lantern down. I'll shew these gentlemen the way. If I want you I will call or send." And, after watching and examining the closed door for a moment, she added: "I am glad you are so patient, Mark;• but it occurs to me that the younger son of an English Earl Must have some deep reason for wishing to remain incognito. Can I help you? Shall I? " This was said with such winning grace that Mark's face, which had been pale and drawn, some- what relaxed, and the colour mounted to his lips and cheeks. I rose to go, but he placed hi:

trembling hand on my arni_ "For somewhat similar reasons to your own," she continued, in the same strain, "reasons which must suggest themselves when you view the Beast, I, too, assumed a false name, for I have an aged mother in Spain, who would break her heart if my misdeeds were known to her. But the evils I have wrought are the exigencies of a romantic/ life; a poor excuse, but one which will shortly appear worthy the consideration of my judges." Mark buried his face in his hands, and with tears trickling down her cheeks Lucia said, in a voice full of emotion: "Come, you shall learn the source of my knowledge of your secret. I got the first inkling at the Quaker's shanty on our way to San Leno. You scattered the pieces of The Times advertisement. I picked them up, saw your descrip- tion and real name. If there was a justification for an unlucky quarrel in your case, when your rival' robbed you of a rich heiress, there will be ample excuse for my crime. Come." He followed her, and I thought of Isaac going to the altar to propitiate. the anger of God. I brought up the rear, cursing my ill-luck, and yet determined not to forsake my friend. Lucia sighed as she unlatched the mortuary door and let us in. There were candles burning, and when she removed the cloth from the still cold face she wept bitterly. Mark steadied himself by seizing my shoulder. The man who had set a price upon my friend's head now lay dead! "When Muro was left to my care," said Lucia, "I nursed him until the nervous irritation caused by his wound considerably lessened. The painful expression of his countenance passed away, the corners of his mouth relaxed, and when ice was continually applied to his spine-the spasms ceased. He soon breathed without sobbing, the muscles of his jaws became less rigid, and at last he was able to open his mouth. The attractions of a roaming life were too strong upon him, and before he properly recovered he proposed moving to the coast. I knew no persuasion of mine could stop him following a set course, and so he went Ms way. It was ever thus with the father of Olive." I put my hand to my palpitating heart and gasped for breath. "Muro her father!" I muttered, looking appealingly at Mark. He was dumb, but I saw that he knew it. "This same restless spirit," continued Lucia, "first brought him into conflict with the people of Golden Vale, and shaped the course of his down- fall. He was prone to give a willing ear to those who falsely spoke of your enmity towards him, and who maliciously saddled you with words you never tittered, and with actions you would despise in any man. Much of this I have learnt since leaving Golden Vale, and I am not a happier woman for my knowledge. It was a strange predestination that you should marry Muro's daughter. We have all sinned; but the Holy Virgin Is merciful, and will forgive." There was a solemn silence, for sadness possessed our souls. "Never mention this to Olive," said the Senorita, when she could command words. "Mark, the jealousy which did the mischief in England was nursed in California. You thought I was Muro's paramour, and yet I dared not explain to you how impossible it was. I held my tongue, he being my eldest brother." "Good God!" I uttered in dismay, "your eldest brother! Then this explains much that puzzled us! " Mark nodded sorrowfully, for he was!unable to utter a word. "Much of my conduct," continued Lucia patheti- cally, "that seemed wilful and even cruel, is now explained. If Muro was wrong, still he was of my flesh and blood; he was my brother, and blood is thicker than water. He was not the author of the robbery of your treasures at Yerba Buena, nor did he, as generally thought,, seize upon your posses- sions when your death was reported, and seemingly confirmed by the eruption of Golden Vale. The knowledge of his relations with Kana I confided to you in order to save his life, even when his grave was dug and the rope about his neck. But for a kindly word from Olive, your wife, I had been too late." "From Olive ?'" reiterated Mark. "From Olive, who is far more clever and just than I gave her credit for. Olive being Kana's daughter, and also a half-caste, always puzzled me until I casually heard that Muro sojourned awhile in Golden Vale when Kana was about seventeen. He married secretly; so Kana's parents banished him and forgave their daughter, making death the penalty for the mention of Muro's name. This explains how Muro obtained Kana's gold cross, which he gave to me at Yerba Buena. And now you shall look upon the man .who, with lies and plausible deceit, poisoned my brother's mind against you. I warn you not to betray us by any exhibi- tion of anger. Come, let us be rid of a gruesome task." 14116£1 shuddered and led the way to the dark death-chamber within the house, carefully, turning her face away as she handed me the lantern and beckoned me to show Mark the features. . "Behold the Brute!" said the Senorita, between her teeth. "The villain can never again see the innocent suffer for the sins of the guilty." , "Sandy," said 'Mark, in a hushed voice, "am I dreaming ? " And turning like a frenzied man towards the Spanish woman he cried: "Lucia, surely this is Harry Puke, once keeper of the tavern, Puke's Delight, Yerba Buena!" The Senorita evidently felt a choking sensation, for she closed her eyes and nodded like one dumb. I examined deceased's chin, and identified a small hard excrescence precisely where Harry Puke had one when I knew him at the tavern. "It is Puke," I muttered, dropping into my mother tongue., "Lat's be rid o' the painful sight. The verra air smells foul." • I nudged Mark, who gladly withdrew with us into the other room. The ordeal had been a fear- ul titnin on bgttla Iducia aecl,44, but :ew we
more zreeiy. mara lapsea into an aim- chair,ci overcome with the weight of these revela- reaz n

tions. t‘l swore upon the graves of our San /*no e 1 said the Sefiorits. when she had placed refreshment m ent for us, that I would track down your enemy, and all my efforts shad failed save for my relations with Puke. Much as I hated his foot- steps and shuddered. at the sound of hia voice, I forced myself to a living death in order to track down the villain. I planted myself upon him as a decoy; I played the coquette, flattered his vanity, spoke ill of you to tempt him, got one of his own heart to report his conversation when inebriated and confiding, and at last wormed out a full confession of how he blackmailed you continually, whereas, after your fearful quarrel with your rival at Oxford, he throttled, killed and robbed that rival. It was not in your interest that Harry Puke c,aine to Yerba Buena, but for fear of detection in.

England." Mark's mind had been at such tension that at the mention of his innocence he broke down and cried like a child. This relieved him, and he muttered some incoherent words of thanks to Lucia for her self-sacrifice, at the same time deploring
_ his short-sightedness. _ "I am terribly deceived in Puke,' he at last commanded words to say calmly; "but much is now made clear that puzzled me. That such revels-

_ tions should ever come out was beyond my expecta- tion; much less that you, Senorita, should be my friend. By an unfortunate misunderstanding you. thought I treated you shamefully when Olive crossed my path; but you must be satisfied that I have somewhat atoned for my follies and expiated mY, sins. God alone knows what I have suffered!" "Yes," replied Lucia tearfully, "that is a con- solation which I cad never claim. In the Brute's death," she added, pointing to the room where Puke's body lay, "the world is rid of a fiend in lambskin. He was all honey till I possessed his secret, and then he wished to be rid of me. •He
killed Muro, and fre-v'enged ray brother's death !" "The vagabond was tied down in the cellar of Puke's Delight as a blind," said I sternly, to Mark. _

"My brother left Yerba Buena in his ship," con- tinued Lucia, "but your treasures were bartered by Puke to any safe buyer who chanced to be leaving the country; and the accusation against Kane was his wilful lie. The treasures were sent to Sacra- mento and stored. Puke was indirectly responsible for the death, of that Indian labourer in the field
- near his saloon, and the faithful Pecos owed his capture to the same man." "And the wretch, no doubt, aided in mine," said I, for the mists were beginning to lift, laying bare the truth.

"I can prove that he planned it," answered Lucia, , "and later on I will also prove to you, by documentary evidence, that by schem- ing and fraud Puke seized your estates. Imagine his wrath, therefore, when, in the last quarrel between • us, I accused him of firing the shots which nearly killed both of us as we danced together on that journey up country. Picture to yourselves my feelings when the Brute mauled my brother in their quarrel near where Mum was found dead. From that spot the wretch under whose roof I lived swaggered home, got drunk, and struck me. I fell against the fender and was stunned. Here upon my left shoulder are the brutal marks of his fist "—she drew aside her dress, and the bruises from his knuckles were

plainly visible—"and behind my ear is the clotted blood and lump caused by the fall. He had not the manliness," she continued bitterly, after moving her hair aside, "to pick me up, but left the negress to find me unconscious. I knew he had killed Alum, and so, when after my recovery I saw him helplessly drunk in his armchair, Satan whispered: 'Kill the monster!' and I was impelled to revenge myself. God forgive me ! I stabbed him to the heart!"

"You must be drearining," said Mark, gazing intently at her haggard face; but' she nodded re- peatedly, as one speechless. "Sefiorita," I observed kindly, realise the enormity of your deed." With an effort she gasped: "I never paused to think of the consequences. Some say Satan has no personality; but I tell you I distinctly heard his voice, and after the deed was done he followed ma behind the curtain, where I sat as one dazed, the while he chuckled. In my fright I dropped my stiletto, and .nothing but presence of mind saved me. As it is, I am fearful what they may worm out of Sarah, for a negress who is threatened is never- to be trusted. You both look incredulous. Yes, it was I who stabbed Puke to the heart!" "Hush!" said Mark with a smothered voice, seizing Lucia in his arms, as she staggered with giddiness. "You must save yourself and all of us! The settlers have already got scent of this!" "Then the negress has betrayed me to them l* she gasped. "You know the summary way they punish in these parts," urged Mark. 'And seeing that Puke killed, Muro, who was hated by the colonists, the man you stabbed will be considered a martyr. What your position is you can guess !" "Will they lynch me?" cried Lucia, her blood- shot eyes dilating till they threatened to start from their sockets. "Not if I can save you," answered Mark. "It will be a lovely night, for the stars begin to shine in a clear sky. You know the trail to Mono. We will bury Muro, and with provisions and sure- footed ponies start under cover of the night." "Upon one condition," said Lucia firmly—"that on nearing your camp I may be allowed to strike off westward, where the immigrants are prospecting for gold. The solitude of the mountains would drive me mad; but amid the excitement and gaiety of some mining camp I will try to smother the past. Come, let us prepare to leave this horrible place." To shield her brother she had lost her lover; to protect her lover she had lost her brother. We busied ourselves during the livelong night with the necessary preparations for a speedy journey, and started with an escort of trusty mot an hour before daybreak, traversing the safer parts of the trail. Lucia camped within easy distance of our rendezvous, determined on striking northward, EO as to fetch the coast, with the Grand Canon of the Tuolumne to her left. Before the parting she gave documentary proofs and verbal details of the transactions of Harry Puke, both in England and California. No mishap had occurred during our short absence, and the saving of our people by Mark's smartness was the most pleasing episode ha our eventful lives. Lucia's going was most affecting; but she bore it with far more cheerfulness than Mark and I. She went forth again among men, to dally with fortune; and ultimately married a rich American of Carson City. We journeyed by easy stages to Sacramento, and Mark's representations to the American Govern- ment secured him a large portion of his confiscated property. Than we joined in the great mining enterprises of the country, with such success that Mark built a large mansion at San Leno, where Olive and her family, faithful Pecos, and sagacious Jip lived to enjoy his prosperity. I travelled several years through Central America, and finally settled in London. lam a hale and hearty old bachelor, enjoying my, declining years with those whose affection I esteem. Nor am I at, all conscious that their attentions are prompted by the knowledge that I have considerable wealth to will them.

div.head: SECRET OF MARK PEPYS.
div.p: SECRET OF MARK PEPYS.
BY FRED J. PROCTOR,
Author of "Timothy Twill's Secret," "Jean
Marlou," ‘Dr. Dobbs." &es
CHAPTER 'XXIX
A SETTLER'S HOSPITALITY.

In a few days the iron ores and auriferous gravels were buried beneath several feet of new snow. The Indian trails over the braes were inaccessible, and we saw few birds save the majestic buzzard. Superhuman aid was required to guide us safely from this ice and snow-bound home; so we had, perforce, to linger prisoners at large where once the mastodon and elephant had freely roamed, while we were fettered by the hand of man. The pioneer miners had not yet invaded pastoral California, to level the foothill forests with fire and axe, and wash out the gulches. The hardiest animals forsook their lairs among the chaparral, and the bears their hiding-places beneath the shelving precipices. Attracted by our fires some visited us and fell easy shots to our marksmen. But soon we belated travellers suffered dreadfully from frost-bite, and ultimately from hunger. Our ponies perished miserably, and were buried beneath the snow before we could finish our cabins in the most sheltered nooks; indeed, we were so hemmed in on every side that starvation stared us in the face. Two Of our sturdiest men volunteered to make for the Tuolumne meadows, hoping to bring food and assistance from settlers. We never saw them

again. 4 After two weary weeks no succour came, and we I had to strip the flesh from the frozen carcases of our mustangs. A third lad undertook a journey to Lake Ten-ai-ya, but, after battling with the snow, he came upon a belated Indi‘n who was reduced to a skeleton and hardly_ able 'rim dr-g .one foot before the other. His account, of the country ahead dis- mayed our man, and both mtinaged to return half- dead. Mv pen cannot adequately describe our sufferings for the next fortnight, nor could a volume of praise do Olive justice. For a woman to be cooped up in that forlorn condition was misery enough, but when she was compelled to boil the skins and bones of our ponies all of us saw we were in desperate straits. Blinding snowstorms, howling tempests, and mighty avalanches added horror to our wretched isolation. Citizens who look out from their cosy rooms and deplore sitOt shower which spoils their pleasure cannot realise the intensity of our sufferings. The boys in the fable were amused as they threw stones into the sedges, but the smitten frogs croaked with pain. So the diversion for Muro and his band meant death for us away in the lonely Sierra. "Sandy," mournfully observed Mark, as he chewed some ox-hide, ‘if this lasts many days some of us may be tempted beyond our power of resistance. We haven't the heart to comb our , hair or pare our nails. If one of us should go mad with hunger, what then? Is there one who would care to become a vampire or ghoul?" The balls of Mark's glistening eyes seemed to start from their sockets at the dreadful thought, and, judging by my feelings, my parchment face must have looked ghastly. I threw him my pouch. He took a pinch of tobacco and actually chewed it to satisfy the gnawing pangs of hunger, saying: "One would imagine we were half-civilised navvies. The nicotine may dull my craving for food." "Three things we hae to be thankful fer," said I, consolingly. "Olive bears adversity wi' exemplary patience, an' we hae abundance o' firewood an' Snow-water. Men hae lived on the latter fer niony -days." I state these things to shew the fearful existence we led. Then an inspiration came. "Saody," said Mark, as I bid him good-night, "if Olive is willing we will start for the south-west at daybreak. Tjse Indian whom we have sheltered tells me that Lucia Diaz has a settlement by the Merced Grove, above the Big Meadows of tose- niite. Our guide knows the trails, and the last few days' frost is lucky for us. Good-night, and Heaven help us." Next morning Mark was in the same frame of . mind, and, moreover, Olive cheerfully acquiesced in his decision. She kept a brave heart when we parted, doubtless preferring to relieve her pent-up feelings in a flood of tears after we had gone. Only an ice-bound party in the Arctic regions could realise our situation ; cut off from civilisa- tion, with little if any chance of communicating our distressed condition to friends; starving, and hourly haunted by the fear of massacre. So far as we know we three explorer.were foraging in the teeth of our enerniese-we ma_C seeking succour at the hands of a woman whose ways were past' my understanding. "This new idea has put new hope into me," observed Mark pluckily, as we filed along after the Indian. "Olive has enough food from our last shot to last her several days, and if it comes to the worst the whole of • them will follow on our track." At every available opportunity we snipped off the end of a branch, split the main member, and wedged the severed part in it. Then where crags abutted on our path we chipped a cross, or erected a tiny cairn of rock tUbris, so that right along our journey were indications for our friends' guidance. Happily the granulated snow, for the most part, bore us, and as we descended into the foothills our guns did good service in providing us with food. I afterwards crossed on horseback from Reno to Wadsworth—that desert-grave of caravan men— when the waste was pallid and lifeless, save for the docks of vultures hovering over a Golgotha of skeletons. I was nearly blinded by the alkaline dust,. and horrified to see nothing but the leaden foliage of the sage-bush, brackish poolg, or slimy rivers where a few lizards crawled. I was silent and forlorn on that accursed track, but my body being in prime condition, I suffered less than on this eventful day, when we were emaciated, and our nerves strained to the utmost tension for the sake of the loved ones left behind. How we crawled on our hands and knees over icy beds, how our feet became sore and our fingers numbed, how, in the lower regions, we were pestered for tobacco by stray aborigines, menaced by the wild men of the forests, and threatened by hungry wolves, are incidents too painful for me to harrow your feelings with. Suffice it that we reached the most outlying settler's cabin beyond Big Oak Flats by five o'clock one evening, hardly able to move. • "Her' ye kern from up country?" asked the brawny settler when he had saluted and welcomed us to seats by his lighted stove. "Prospectin' like ? " Mark nodded. "Here, redskin, none o' yer darned kempany ef titer ain't work in ye. Find suthin' to do; demme, tak' this fish an' toast 'n. Ef 'e wants .a shake down let 'n earn it," con- tinued the voluble but hospitable settler, rubbing his bushy whiskers and then his big brown- hands. "Wot shall it be, strangers, a dish o'tea or a basin o' broth ? " "We prefer a cup of coffee with a dash of brandy in it," said Mark, as he brushed the snow from his boots before taking them off. "Ye kin bet ver life," grinned the busy host, "diet a drop o' San Leno's old stock is good, real tipeiop stuff. An' ninny a bottle I've put away dose I'd tale fever down along the Sacramento. And sniffing the Indian he added, grumpily: "Tisk' care, redskin, I reckon ye'll burn diet SA into a shrivel. Guess ye should stand twice the journey an' not look so woe-begone." "The truth is," explained Mark, while the settler was dashing down the cups and plates on his worn fir table, "we've been cooped up for weeks in the Sierras and half starved." "lies' ye now," responded the sympathetic man; "then I calkilate a good feed won't. kern amiss. I judged, by the look o' yer frier-id, ez he'd been livin' on skewers fer six months." This referred to my attenuated frame. "Still, Lord Nelson was a spare man. . . . Look-oat, thar! the coffee's- bilin' overt Jest my nigger-luck. Sugar an' milk, both on yer? " We nodded, and the settler poured a drop of brandy in the three cups, saying, as he patted the bottle: "In darned good fettle, this ; bottled afore Mark Pepys owned the ranch, when Father Otando bossed the show fer the Govern- ment. I once worked at San Lent). but never see'd the gov'nor, as he stuck to Yerba Buena. They do say ez how be were well-connected, an' a darned pow'fill chap, but he couldn't keep cl'ar o' filet Spanish gel. . . Thet's right! Glad to see yer tuckin' in hearty like. I al'ays thinks-thar's suthin' wrong ef a man can't eat." Mark svrilted at me fuel smiled, for we were too Duey appeasing our hunger to talk, if, indeed, our host had permitted a word in edgeways. He was cominneicative, and we enjoyed his chatter, as it 4ave m the opportunity to eat. "By the way, ye've kern iu dime fer a sensation. Yesterday, Mr. What's- his-nause, cz hoped the saloon down Sacramento

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. THE NEW BILL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. THE NEW BILL.

A special meeting of the Council was held on ! Tuesday evening, commencing shortly after five o'clock, "for the purpose of considering and, if thought fit, oZ passing a resolution that the Town Ceuncil do promote a Bill in the next Session of Parliament for the construction of additional water- works and the improvement of the borough of Warrington, and for other purposes." The Mayor presided, and there were also present the Deputy- Mayor (Alderman Fairclough), Aldermen Roberts, Blackhurst, Bolton, and Hutchinson • Councillors Shaw Green, Smethurst, Bennett, James Evans, Ellison, Cannel!, Plumpton, John Evans, Duncan, Tinnion, Baird, Peacock, Jolley, Lnogton,Shillcock, Wilkinson, F. W. Monks, R. Heaton, J. Lee, John Roberts, F.R.Rohsrts; Messra.J Lyon Whittle(Town Clerk),Stanley Wilson(Deputy Town Clerk), J. Deas (water engineer), W. S. Haddock (Gas Engineer), T. Longd,in (Borough Surveyor),and J.6utcliffe (assistant Borough Surveyor). The MAYOR said it was for the Council that nieht to confirm the resolution, and then a meeting of the rate- payers would be called to ask their approval of the Bbl, and then the matter would again be brought before the Council far confirmation. Councillor Saes, GREEN Are there sufficient mem- bers present ? The TOWN CLERK: There is not an absolute majority of the Council, but the resolution caa be passed at the end of the meeting, when no doubt taura members will be present. The MAYOR: There can be no voting upon the matter at present. The Council then resolved itself into Committee, and while the clauses of the Bill were being discusses other members put in an appearance. It was dacided to discuss the claugee seriatim. ADDITIONAL WATERWORKS. LARGE EXPENDITURE.

Councillor LEE. as of the Water Com- mittee, said the Council, had had an opportunity of studying the Bill. An effort Was to be made to meet the need for more water. The growth of the population had te be taken into consideration. Twenty years hence they calculated that the population would be double what it was now for the water area, and that was sufficient reason for providing a scheme such as that proposed. The scheme had been suggested by Mr. Mansergh (the eminent water engineer) and involved an increase of the supply at Winwick, and an increase could be made at a comparatively stnall expense. They had to consider the question of supp.ying the out- districts that were not supplied now, and that was part of the Winwick scheme—thosa distri baing within the water area. The consumption of watga. from Appleton was also growing in such a rapid manner that they wonld be in a precarious condition there before long if some im- provements were not made. The coneumption of water for manufacturing purposes in 1891. was 74i, millien gallons, and now it was estimated at more than 100 mil- lion gallons, and they wanted more storage during the winter. The cost of the undertaking was put down at £2.82,000, but it did not follow that all that money would he spent neccssarily. Tney would only spend what they required, Their object as aVe at,r Commit- tee was to avoid putting on a water rate. (Hear, hear.) They had discusvd the matter that day at a private meeting, and they were satisfi d that with judicious management they could make the improvement which were absolutely necessary within the next five or seven years without at all burdening the rates. Their revenue had increased so rapidly and so steadily that they were justified in saying that they would not have to levy a rate at all. (hear, hear.) They had every o)afidenee in Mr Deas that he would deal with the matter in a piecerroal sort of manner, as necessary. What they wanted was to be able to provide a sufficieet supply of water. Although they might do witaout gas for a few days, they conld not do without water, and they wanted to provide against any emergency. The Boreueh Treasurer told them that they could commence as soon as they got the Bill, and spend £50.000 without affect- ing them in the least, as far as dractring on any reserve was concerned. _ . _

---COU-n-cilIo.;-§-ar- Beeman said he had heard it said that by spending seine thousands of pounds at Win wick there was sufficient water to be found to supply them for ano'har 100 years. Was that so ? If so, ha should be loath to spend any money in- Councillor SRAW GREEN : So would anyone else. Councillor SMETRoRST : Very well. You can have your say by-and-by, when I have done. Ccatieuicg,he said he gave the Water Committee credit for Laing care- ful, but there was an impression in Warringtoa that they had spent money for a long time with the expecte- tion that they would have some revenue from the Water Works, but that expectation bad been knocked entirely from under their feet, and they must give up expectine any revenue for the pre3ent. In a few years he was told they might expect a revenue of some thousands 01 pounds. Was it correct, he again aQked,that by sinking another well and putting in a Dumping station there would be'sufficiant water for 100 years to come ? Councillor BENNETT said that he had read the Bitt carefully, and he was staggered when he came to the amount proposed ,to be spent for water purposes. In his ci dest dreems he had never contemplated an ex- penditure so huge ae that tor some years to come. They had been told by Councillor Lee that these huge im- prcvements could be undertaken without any addition to the rates, but he must confess that he wag &rase enough not to s!e how that could be possible if they spent anything like the whole of the amount which had b.en named. Tbe prospect was very remote of getting that relief from the rates by the nroits on the Water Works which they • had anticipited unless they used the , greatest care. It was, he admitted, essential that they I should have a first-rate water supply, and it was not business if there was any demand for water not to b 3 in a position to cope-with the demand, but was it not possib'e to secure these ends without meking such a gigantic plunge all at once? Could they not proceed with the matter step by step? The MAYOR That is the intention. We are asking you to give us permission to obtain poweri to carry out the work. 3ouncillor BENNETT : We are obliged to carry out the work within seven years. The MAYOR: Not absolutely. Councillor LEE: We must de it in seven years steak for renewed powers. Councillor BENNETT : That is prac' What I say. It would be much wiser to go tor smatter powers at present. Alderman ROBERTS stated thet the Bill was a very comprehensive one, and he confessed it justified the question which Councillor Bennett had put. It was in- tended to do the work in sections, and to spread the expenditure over the whole period mentioned in the Bill and not te proceed with any portion of the work which in the opinion of the committee might be capable of modification or improvement within the time; in other veerds they proposed to abandon any portion which later experience might prove to them was tmlesirable. If they found that they could not comp ete the whole echeme within the period named they could go to Par- liament for ae exten3ion of time. There would be no difficulty in applying for a renewal of the powers and this renewal of powers could be got at a very limited cost irdeed. Fortunately er nnfortunataly, the neeessi- ties of the town, domestic and commercial, had grown at such a rate that they must provide for the increase.

They must be satisfied for a few years to allow the pro- fit on the water undertaking to be used as a means for borrowing the capital sum necessary for the extensions. They hid worked the scheme out for the first the or four yeare, and anticipating the incl.° teed revenue to go on pre rata, they had no hesitation in saying that the first four years portion of the scheme coeld be carried out without burdening the towu to the extent of a penny in the shape of a rate. (Hear, hear.) On the other hand,their anticipated profit he must admit would be mortgaged for the purpose. and instead of being able to hand over during the next four years 21.000 or £1,500 per annum in relief of tbe rates,if they proceeded with the scheme they would have to bold that money in hand as their justificatlon for borrowing the capital sum necessary for the extensions. They could not stop the growth of the population, nor bad they any desire to do so. They had no desire to stop the commercial interests, and they wished to be in a cosition to offer every facility to the present and to future concerns that might be introduced into Warrington as a home. To do that they must anticipate to some extent the n,c,eoitiea * so far as the water was concerned—the necessities of the population and the commercial undertekings, (Hear, hear.) It was with that object in view that they were bringing forward this Bill. They had been in a position once or twice of being perilously near a shortage of water, and they were determined not to allow that condition of things to occur again. The powers sought for were necessary and desirable. The MAYOR : We are not absolutely bound to the engineer's scheme as set forth. Alderman ROBERTS Not at all. We can alter or modify in any way we think fit. The scheme comprises three things—the extension of the supply at Winwick, the construction of a small—comparatively small-- reservoir at Asnnow,and a large reservoir at Paresbury. We can proceed with ene, two, or three, simultaneously or 'otherwise, as we think fit. Courcillor BENNETT : Shen years appears to be such a short time. The MAYOR That is fixed by Parliament. Councillor BENNETT : And it cannot be extended. The MAYOR: No. Councillor SMETRIIRST remarked that two or three of the largest consumers of water who used to be supplied from Hill Cliffe had given over taking water from the Corporation. (" No, no.") Messrs. Pearson and Knowles and Mevrs. Crosfield for instance. (Further Cries of " No. no.") Alderman ROBERTS: Pearson and Knowles did in the time of the old company. There WAS then considerable friction.
" LINSEED CONIMUND " for Chingos and Colds, allays irritation. Ulna immediate relief.— Advt.

Councillor Siam GREEN : It was a good job for us they did so. Althrmari ROBERTS : We could not supply them at present. The TOWN CLEkx Mr. Deas sap they will cone back—all of them. Councillor BENNETT drew special attention to Clause 41, which was as follows :—"The Corporation shall not under the powers of this part of the Act purchase or acquire in any city, borough, or urban district, or any parish or part of a parish not being witlin the urban district, ten or more houses which on the 15th day of December last wero or have since that day, or shall here- after, be occupied either wholly or partially by perms belonging to the labouring classes as tenants or loigers." He quite agreed that if any of the working classes were ousted from their dwellings it was the absolute duty of the Corporation to find them other homes equally com- fortable. It seemed to him that by this clause they would not be able to deal with any property. It might operate very injuriously. Tue TOIVN CLERK said the clause was insertel by one of the standing orders of the House. Councillor BENNETT remarked that it woul4 be ridicul- ous to turn them out, but if they provided them with suitable accommodation elsewhere it would not. THE HEIGHT OF CHIMNEYS. __

_ Clause 52 contained the following :—" All chimneys hereafter erected far carrying any smoke from the fur- nace of any mill, factory, brewery, sizing house, dye house, gas works, corn mill, foundry or buildings wed for manufacturing purposes, or for the carrying away of any nols3rne or deleterious gasses or effluvia from any such buildings, shall b 3 raised t 3 the height of 50 feet at least from the level of the centre of the street nearest thereto, and in all cases where any chimney serves the furnace of a steam engine the chimney shall be raised to an additional height from such level adapted to the power of such engine according to the following scale (that is to say) : If such steam engine be of more than ten horse power and do not exceed thirty horse power the height of such chimney shall not be less than eighty fe3t ;if such st.am engine be more than thirty horse power and do not exceed forty horse power the height of such chimney shall no be less than one hundred and ten feet, and if such steam engine be mere than forty horse power the height of such chimney shall not be less than one hundred and twenty feet." Aldermau BOLTON thought it was rather hard that people should be tied to have their chimneys such a height. It was decided that the Parliamentary Committee ahould reconsider the clause.

The Tows CLERK drew atzention to the last para- graph of clause 55 which was ae follows: "In esti- mating the amount of c mmensation or purchase moaev to be paid by the Corporation under this Act the bene- fits accruinz to the person to whom the same shall be paid by reason of the widening or the impzovf-ment of any street shall be fairly estimated, and shall b 3 set off against the said compeosation or purchase money." Alderman BOLTON ask 'd if the clause would apply to all works. If a shed were t 3 be erected would plans be required ? The Tows CLERK: It does not say anything about plans. Alderman BOLTON did not want it to be So stringent that it would interfere with the manufacturers of the town. They wanted a certain amount of latitude, which a jerry builder ought not to have. The clause was referred back to the committee for re- consideration.
THE POWERS OF THE STREET IMPROVEMENT COMMITTEE.

Cause 74- requires persons washing or man.cling clothes to furnish list of omen of clothes in certain cases, and Clausc. 76 made it incumbent upon cowkse.pers and ethers to furnish lists of customers in csrtain cases. Alderman ROBERTS said those clauses would b 3 put into opEntion if the Medical Officer satisfied the Corpor- ation or the Health Committee that it was des'rable to do so with a view to preventing the spread of infectious disease. They would not be put into operation unless there was an outbreak already in existence which it was desirable to check.
PAYMENT OF PUBLIC BANDS.-THE QUESTION

OF A HALIIPENNY RITE. Clause 101. read as foil )ws :—"The Corporation may from time to time pay or contribute out of the improve- ment rate towards the payment of pantie band or binds of music to perform in any public park, garden. or recreation ground, or other place of public resort within the borough belonging to or held by the Corpora- tion, and the Corporation may enclose an area within which such band shall play, and may make, alter, and repeal bylaws for regulating the time and place for the playing of the band and the payments to be made for admission within the said enclosure, and for securing gcol and orderly conduct dnring the playing of the band. Provided that the amount of such payment or contribution by the Corporation for or towards such band dull not in any one year exceed an amount which would be produced by a rate of one-halfpenny in the pound on the assessable value of the borough to the im- provement rate."

- Alderman BOLTON thought the Clause should be struck out. They rave the bands £5O a year and a halfpenny rate meant £3OO a year at least. He did not think they were justified in levying a rate for the sake of public bands. They had no right te put: on another rate. The TOWN CLERK : It doesn't fix a rate. Alderman BOLTON : It says so. The TOWN CLERK: It only restricts your expenditure. Before you had no legal right to pay to the bands. Alderman BouroN : A farthing is sefficient. He pro- posed that a farthing be put in the clause. Councillor Dr. CANNELL said the Bands Association had not asked for the money, and they did not want it. They were perfectly satisfied with £5O. Alderman ROBERTS supported the proposal in the chose. He said that it did not pledge the Corporation to spend anyttling more, but fired the maximum they were capaWe of spending. When they loelted at the condition of Warrington, a manufacturing town, where the life of the people was necessarily dull, it was the duty of the Corporation and the privilege of the Corpor- ation to offer as many facilities as they , could for the brightening of the lives of the people. He would sup- port the clause on that ground alone. He was quite sure that public spirit wan largely in the direc'ion of proeiding facilities for enjoyment and recreation. He asked them not to let Warrington play second fiddle to any other town in the country. Of course the commit- tee in giving the £5O hal done what legally they had no right to do, but it had had the support of the town. This clause would simply put them in a legal position, and limit their expenditure. If they did not want to spend the whole they could limit it to a farthing. Let them not b 3 cheese-Paring in this policy of providing reasonable and rational recreatim in the town. (Hear, itear.) Councillor BENNETT supported what Alderman Roberts had said. He did not thiek they could spend the money of the Corporation in a better way. Conncillor HEA.TON.Said he should not like it to go to th 3 public that the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Com- rraittee had given the money without authority. Alderman ROBERTS: I didn't say so. Counciller HEATON We had the authority of this Council. Alderman ROBERTS: I said the committee had the support of this Council and the public opinion of the town,but the act was ot a leeal one Councillor HEATON : Alderman Roberts said it was an illegal act and they had no right to do it. I agree to the bands having something, but I don't see that we should extract from the ratepayers £3OO a year. The MAYOR: It will always be M your hands to say what you will give. The Tower CLERK said that no rate was fixed. Alderman Booecne said they would have to levy the rate and neeple would come to them and say "You have £3OO a year for this,and we want this and we want the other." Councillor SHAW GREEN said the matter of the amount would be entirely in their own hands. Alderman ROBERTS observed that the committee would have power to spend a sum of money not to exceed what a halfpenny in the pound would raise, but they could in their discretion, spend less. Councillor HEATON Do I understand that we need not give more than £5O or £6O. The TOWN CLERK: That is so. Alderman BOLT3N'S nropositiol evaa put to the vote, anal lost, a large majority voting against. The clause was then confirm,d.

PROPOSED COLLECTION OF TIE POOR RATE BY TtlE COLIPORATiON. Clauses 113 and 11.4 gave toe Corporation power to take over the collection of the poor rate. Councillor BENNETT relied the cpestien of the compose- sation of Mr. Tunstall provided the Cerporatioa took over those duties. Councillor &Lew GREEN stated that the Act laid down that way official who lost his appointment shouLd be compensate 1. Counciller BENNETT : Does that include his staff? Councillor SHAW GREEN : Ido not think, so. Alderman ROBERTS siid the question raised by Coue- cillor Bennett was a very imeerta.nt one, and one about which the Council should be quite clear. It (seemed to him that Mr. Tunstall's appointment was an individual appointment, and there were only two ways of estimat- ing the compensation to be paid to him One was to re- gard it as a personal appointment, ani compensate him upon the gross emoluments he received, or taking it as an individual appointment deduct from it the exeess of his official staff and compensate him upon the basis of the remeinier and the Corporation to take over the offi- cial staff. The MAYO 2 said he thought that was what the sub- committee had in tonic minds. Councillor BENNETT : I take it the shaff will be treated equitably and fair. Alderman ROBERTS said he did not think there were two opinions as to the desirability of the Corporation taking over the power of collecting the poor rates. There was more involved in he proposal than that. In the poor rate office the Borough lists were prepared. Toe work of rate collector involved the duties of asdstant overseer as well. Mr. TunstalPs utaff,be took it.did not come under tee defiuition of "other officials" as defined in the bill, but what Was perfectly patent to his mind was that they must compensate Mr. Tuastall on the basis of it beinga personal appointment if they wee not going to take over his staff, or take over his staff and compensate him on the net amount.' (Hear, heir.) Councillor SHAW GREEN said negotiations had brae entered into with Mr. Tunstall. It was incredible in this day that they should have two rates books to do the work of ons, and two collectors going round the tesvu one upon toe heels of the other, seeing that they had obtained certain pOwers from the Local Govern- ment Board. They wanted to go a step further and collect the rates together. They were eneeavaur.ne to do what was reasonable an 1 proper in the matter, and they bad approached Mr. Tess all t see if he was will- ing on reasonable terms, to give up his appointment. Tney were still negotiating. They wanted to do what was strictly just and fair to Mr. Tunstail. Councillor Monies said he believed Warrington was the only town woera rates were collected in their pre- sent way by the Assistant Overseer. In a2ost towns the Assistant Overseer superintended the collection, but so far as he (Couacillor Monks) knew, Mt. Tunstell did not do the work himself. fie farmed the office out to clerks and aEsistants. In considerieg the question of corn pen- sation that should have a strong bearing on the subj,,cs. Councillor SHAW GREEN said if the Corp oration desired to take the work over they would have to do so on terms acceptab:e to the Assistant Overseer. Alderman HUTCHINSON thought the officials of the Cor- poration had enough work t 3 do, and prop hie 1 that the clause be expuuged. There was no seconder, and the clause was anp roved. PROPOSED TLIRIFF FUND.—AN OBJECTION. Alderman BOLTON asked how much the thrift fund in the Bill would cost the retepapere, and who was the father of it. [he Tower CLERK said they were now only asked to affirm the principles of the Bill. Alderman BoLeoe said be did not understand it, and he did not want to affirm it. It meant tow were going to have more rates. Councillor SHAW GREEN said he did not know who was the father of the scheme, but be was satisfied with it. It was an attempt on the part of the Corporaeion to pro- vide an allowance for their workpeople. Councillor SURTHURST : Exactly. A. pension out of the rates. They have been trying a good many years for that. Alderman BOLTON wished to have further information. Councillor SHAW GREEN said the amount of wages paid by the Corp oration was £4OO a week. The proposal was that the Corporation should contribute 4 per cent; that was £lO a week. They wanted to corns into line with other Corporations and every big institution. Councillor PEACOCK said he understood that 24 per cent would be ;laid by the Corporation, and 2i per coat by the workprople. Councilor SHAW Gas Es replied in the affirmative. The DEPUTY-MAYOR : We have the same thing at the Police St stion. Alderman BOLTON: But the Government contributes to it. The clauses were approved. NEARLY HALF A MILLION TO BE SPEN.P. Co ncillor BEsserre said the tot al sum whice they pro- posed to obtain powers to have the right of borrowing was £418,000, an enormous sum. They ought to kesp the expenditure down as much a 3 possible, though the amount preposed to be spent for a Tenni :al School— £l4,ooo was, in his opinion, too little. The Towei CLERK said then would be no charge upon the rates for the water. In answer to Councillor Heaton Councillor SHAW GREEN said the total indebtedness of the town at the present time was £580,000,bu- they had gas and water undert drier', markets, tee Town Hall and Municipal Offices and many other v.iluable assets to set against that. POWERS OF BORROWING MONEY. The Tows CLERK read Clause 126, as follows :—" The powers of borrowing money by this Act given shall not be restricted by any of the regulation's contained in sec- tion 234 of the Public Health Act, 1875, and in calculat- ing the amount which the Corporation may borrow under that Act or under any other eaacterient relating to the Corporation any sums which they may bcrrow under thia ket shall not be reckoned." Mr. Whittle explained, in answer to Councillor Bennett, that that was a clause which was put in every Act. They could not borrow more than twice the assessable value of the borough. Councillor BENNETT : This extends the amount we are borrowing under these specific heads. The Tows CLERK : You are taking power to borrow. Councillor BENNETT : But that takes no account of the money you borrow under the Public Health Att. I want us to face the matter frankly, and to know where we are going. The clause was agreed to. The 'rows CLERK said Clause 137 was a new one :- 4. Where the Corporation are authorised by ay statu- tory borrowing power to raise money for any purpose by the issue of mortgage bonds, or mortgages, or by the creation or issue of a Corporation stock,the Corp oretion, instead of exercisine such borrowing power by the crea- tion and issue of additional bonds, •or mortgages, or stock, may exercise the said power and raise the said money either wholly or partially by using for such pier- poaes any money for the time being forming part of the redemption fund." Councillor SHAW GREEN: These are clauses to assist us in dealing with the capital debt. The Tows CLERK : But they are new clauses. The Council agreed to the new clauses. BURIAL FEES. The Tows CLERK explained that Clause 142 enabled the Corporation to enter into agreement with vicars and clerk; for the commutation of burial fees. Alderman BOLTON:: TWO is all right. (Laughter.) Approved. POWER TO EN FEB BURNING BUILDINGS. Clause 152, the Tows CLERK explained, gave power to the police to enter premises in case of fire. All the rest were the usual clauses. Alderman BOLTON: Have we not always had that power? The TOWN CLERK : No, sir. Alderman BoLeox : I always understood we had. Alderman HIITCOINSON : Have firemen not always had that riermissiem ? The TOWN CLERK: No, sir. There ha a never been any difficulty, but this elves us the legal power. COUNCILLOR MONKS AND THE TOWN CLERK. The MAYOR then proposed "That the Town Council do promote a Bill in the 'text session of Parliament for the construction of additional %ewer works and the im- provement of the borough of Warrington and for other purposes." Councillor Moents seconded the preposition, and said he should like to tike that opportunity of. saying a few words in connection with the Bill as a whole. He had srne hesltttion in doing so because what he might have to say might reflect some little on the methods which had been adopted in the preparation of the Bill, and as such on the Town Clerk himself. But he hoped the Town Clerk would not take it as a personal matter. He did his work generally remarkably well, but in this per- Iticular case a number of previsions had been included in the Bill without consulting the committees most directly interested. Take the clause referring to the erection of a Technical Institute. That was a mater that had been put in the Bill without the Museum or Institute Com- mittee being consulted. The Tower CLERK: The Finance Committee were consulted. • Councillor MONKS: But the committee directly con- cerned should have been consulted. The Tows CLERK : The Finance Committee find the money. ' Councillor MONKS: It would have been more bud- neaa like if the different matters had boon put before the different committees. It only seems reasonable. The Tower CLERK: In answer to that I may say that all the provisions relating to new strsets were submitted to the Street Improvement Committee, and sanitary re- gulations and infectious disease maters to the Health Committee, and were approved by them. Councillor MOs: I am only speaking of these matters which have not been put before the committee concerned. The motion was then put to the meeting and agreed to unanimously. THE ORDINARY MEETING. Councillor BENNETT moved an amendment with regard to the resolution" that the plans showing the line of frontage in certain str .ets be signed and deposited." He said a large number of streets were affected by the pro- posal line of frontage. He was not present when the particular frontages were fixed, and be did not think it was fair to the Council that they should be adepts d without having the plans suspended in the ro-un. They affected streets like Buttermarket-street. Sankey-street, and Horsemarket street ; and fixed the line for all time. He thought the Counoil should have an opportunity of judging wlut the proposed street lines were. He should tie glad if the chairman of the committee could sea his way to withdraw the matter until the next meeting of the Council. _ _

The TOWN CLERK : It cannot be withdrawn. The notices hive been served. It is to prevent the erection of certain buildings. Cquacillor 13EssErr : It ig a great mistake. We are making most momentous changes and the Council knows nothing. The MAYOR: They have been approved by the com- mittee. _ _ _

Councillor BENNETT thought they had not. The TowN CLERK: The Council passed a resolution that the main streets should be widened to 601 t. and the secondary streets to 50fc. The plans were submitted to the Street Improvement Committee. Alderman BLACESURST : I rise to a point of order. If Councillor Bennett does not know he ought to know, as he is a member of the committee. Councillor BENNETT : It is not fair to bring a compre4 hensive scheme of suck public importance before the Cowie 1 and pass it without the Council knowing what they are doing. Toe MAYOR. The lines are strictly in accordance with the resolution of the Council, and have been ap- proved by the Street Improvement Committee. C4uocillor MoNics said alit the members of the Coun- cil, outside the committee, had had no opportunity yet of making themselves acquainted with the plans. Could they not be held over until next month? It was d-cided that the plans be sent for. In the meantime other bus Mess was taken, and just before the Council rose the plans, which had been in the room some time, were again alluded 0 by Councillor Bennett, who moved that the question be deferred for a month. It was not carried however, and the minutes were con- firmed with the slight alteration suggested by Cbuncillor Blackhurst.

The thath rate is lower, and birth rate higher, but the zymotio rate is slightly higher, bat as it was what is called ' A. diarrhee t year,' the death rate from this disease aloaill being 2.02 per 1,000, I think the Health C3mmittee may not exactly rest and be thankful, but continue their good work until the general death rate is 15 and ZyMOtie One. 1889: Detth rate per 1,000 of population, 17 87; birth rate, 3756; zc-rnotic (seven chief zymotics), 329 ; diarrhoea alone, 2.02; total deaths from diarrhart, 127; and out of this numher 87 were un- der one year of age." The figures for 1897 were given, showing that the death rate was 15 5. and the Nitta rate 361, the zyrnotic death rate 28. INQUEST.

On Tuesday afternoon Mr. Worsley (coroner) held an inquest on the body of William Brocklehurst, cartet,(29) residing at 5. Cliffa View, Walton Inferior, in the cm- ploy of Mr. Stanley Carter, Warrington, and who died on Sunday morning about 3-30.—John Weave, a retired farmer, and residing at 5, Cliffe View, and father-itelaw to the deceased said on the Saturday night about 10 o'clock be went to bed leaving his son-in-law getting his supper. He bad never beard him complain, and had lived with him abseet three sears. The deceased had had some extra work lately. The deceased's wife was, awakeried,by hearing him struggling as though restless, ' and was unable to arouse him. He had had nightmares before,but she had always been able to waren him —Dr. , Samuel Parker, M.D., pract'sing in Stockton Heath said he had had no previous knowledge of the deceasee at any time. He was called in on the morning of the let January and found him dead. It was about 430 a.m. Witness had made an external examination and had seen the wife who was not fit to come out, and heard her story. He believed the death was due to syncepre brought about by his hard w eek's work. He did no suppose it followed there was anythine wrong with his heart, but deceased must have had a weak pulse, which would be an indication of nervous exhaustion.—ln reply to the Coroner the jury said they did not think it necessary to call Mrs. Brockkhurst as she was ill, and returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidecce.—The Cororer said it was a singu- lar fact that this was the fourth iequest he had held in the last fortnieht on people who had died from sudden failure of the heart or syncope% in this way. He was sure he was expressing the feelings of all when he said they felt very sorry for the widow in the sudden blow she had sustained.
