JUST now some of our con- The Spoils of temporaries are disposed to be Office.

querulous because honours and titles are being bestowed upon men who have served the Government party in various ways. These displays of virtue seem to be rather fantastic when it is remembered that Lord HEE-. SCHELL was so often blamed for bestowing his pa- tronage so impartially as to leave out Liberals. The truth is that our party system implies the distribution of the spoils on party lines, and it is hard to find fault with it. What we do have to say in the matter, looking on with the impartial ob- servation of an outsider,is that whilst the Conserv.-..-- tives reward their adherents and spokesmen web, regardless of the merits of opponents, the Liber :3 are far too apt to invite the world to admire their impartiality, and to neglect good Liberals in con' sequence. The system of spoils can only be defensible on one ground that it is legitimate, inevitable, and practised by each party in turn, without any sacrifice of ' national interests. It does not matter much wl-ether a judge has been a Liberal or a Conserv.- tive. It matters a good deal whether a lawyer, who has given good service to his party, and has entered Parliament frequently at his own expense, shall be secure of promotion when a suitable opportunity arrives. So of wealthy men who want titles. It has been often alleged that Patronage Secretaries on the Liberal side have been fastidi- ous and neglectful, driving the ambitions over to the other side. A man likes to be recognised for what he is worth, and if the party system is to go on that party will advance most which is fairest to its adherents, and looks best after its professional, wealthy, and humbler followers. We are not ad- vocating corruption, but a legitimate system of re- wards. The Liberal party cbustantly suffers be- cause it will not look after Liberals. It concerns itself with a mixed display of high party virtue and public disinterestedness. It receives blame in the one case for neglect, and obtains no credit in the other for its principle of selection. The lessons of the last few years are making a deep impression on the public mind. We see that the spoils of office are being freely bestowed amongst the supporters of the present Government. At rare intervals some Liberal is honoured, but titles, places, appointments, rewards, go to Unionists in the majority of nine- teen to one. The example is one the Liberals will have to follow when next they are in office. They must have a Lord Chancellor who will remember his own family and his own party. They must have a Patronage Secretary who will make a point of rewarding party men and men who have done good service, instead of sending them empty away. They must have members who will sur- round themselves by Liberal young men in their offices, and a Premier who will not hesitate to recommend Liberal clergymen and barristers for high appointments. Anything short of this will neither be good policy nor obei-Ni ence to party principles. The moral is so obvious to everybody that it is time the newspapers spoke out upon the subject, and let leaders see what is running in the minds of their followbrs.
THE. introductim of a submarine Naval Warfare, boat is being regarded by some _

persons as likely to revolutionise naval warfare. The assumption seems to us to be wholly unwarranted. The naval boat France is making will do some remarkable things. It will sink below the surface of the water and remain there for some time. It will fire a torpedo under water at an object which has been sighted as to position and distance from the surface of the water. Its oftensiVeness is thus limited to torpedo- firing after a calculation has been made on the surface. Probably daylight would be required for this calculation, as accuracy could not be ensured without it. What, ther, does a submarine boat add to ordinary naval risks? The answer is, Nothing. The boat may make one or two dives be- fore it comes up for the final survey. The act of coming up, the sighting, and the going under again will require about five minutes Assuming the time to be daylight, the attacked ship would have about five minutes to gat ready for the counter attack. It could shell the boat, and pour upon it the firo of its quick firing guns, at a range of probably not more than from four to s;x hundred yards. The ordinary torpedo-boat would be within sight for a longer period before it reached the point whence its torpedo would be fired. The advantage of the submarine boat is that this period of being within sight would be lessened. Still if a sharp look out were kept the submarine boat would be seen to make the last dive but one before sighting for its torpedo dis- charge, and the stationary ship would have to fire a series of shells and round shot along tha path which the submarine boat must take If this were done the probability is that the submarine boat would never be seen again. A very slight injury to its mechanism would pre vent the boat rising, and any real hit might ex-.

div.p: plode the torp3do under water. The attacking boat is thus just as likely to be a death-trap for everybody in it as to be a new source of anxiety. Ably against stationary ships would the submarine boat have any chance of . favourable attack. Against a moving ship the final calculations be- fore sinking down to fire the torpedo might be readily disturbed by the moving ship going on an- other course. The submarine boat cannot remain under water long, it cannot sight anything under water, it can only fire a torpedo; and therefore its attacking power is very limited, and the dangers it has to encounter are greater than are presented to the crew of a surface-steaming torpedo-boat, which may be, when in range, a target for the enemy, but runs no risk of destruction out of sight by missiles dropping round it in the sea. In fact, it may be said with confidence that the first time a submarine boat, fairly seen, presumes to at- tack a British man-o'-war, it will be a su4rmarine boat thenceforth and for ever.

The parliamentary vacancy in the N ewton Divi- sion has every appearance of providing Colonel Richard Pilkington with a comfortable walk-over. Influential Liberals with more than a modicum of pluck seem to be rare in the division, for not one can be found who will seek the suffrages of the electors in the Liberal interest. The Committee of the Liberal Three if does not seem to ' have been inactive, but rather the reverse, for strenuous efforts have been made to secure a can- didate, though unfortunately without avail. We are greatly disappointed with the Newton Liberals, and a little bit disgusted with those 'hose apathy for the cause or lack of courage impels them to avoid the challenge thrown out by Colonel Pdkington. Of course the odds are on the Conservative side, but the only way in which this fact should be considered is in the light of providing an opportunity for aso much handsomer victory. The same condi- tion of things obtains in the Aylesbury Division, where local Liberalism is over awed by the Rlths- child might and millions. Newton Division is by no means a forlorn hope, and a sound, influential, local Liberal would have had the rosiest of chances against Colonel Pilkington. The latter seems to have a very exalted idea about the virtues of the present Government, and a very faint comprehen- sion of its weaknesses, but the views he so confi- dently expresses ale by no means shared in by electors all over the division. Even now a cour- ageous Liberal might take the field, and find sufficient support to make this candidature a suc- cess complete and absolute. But the chance is apparently going to be allowed to slide, and any- thing more harmful to Liberalism in New ton Division could not be imagined.

Between Mr. Bennet Barleigh and Mr. E. N. Bennett there is a not very pretty quarrel proceed- ing anent the authenticity of statements alleging that the wounded dervishes at Omdurman were kilted by soldiers under the British flag. So far as we can judge from all that has been said and written about such a serious matter, the charge Was not entirely groundless. We should be very reluctant to admit that even the coloured allies of the British troops were guilty of such savagery as is imputed, for they are part and parcel of the English army. But it is difficult to imagine such assertions being _made without some foundation upon fact. The charge has been emphatically denied in official qiiarters, and revived in others which may be considered qnte as reliable. What the truth of the matter is we cannot quite deter- mine, and we shall have to wait and see the out- come of the quarrel between the two correspon- dents mentioned, which may or may not throw 8. ome light on the question, but our present feeling is that some of the wounded dervishes, whether malevolently inclined or not, received scant mercy from their conquerors.

A seven days'railway race between the Chicago and Quincy line on the one hand and the North- Western line on the other, has fortunately °come to a conclusion without disaster. The prize is a Government mail contract, which is perhaps the most as. tonishing fact of all. When Governments patronise dangerous and unseamly races it is unreasonable to expect the common people to do otherwise. In Spain and Portugal Government Patronises bull-fiahtina) and the people follow suit. n n In America Government patronises railway racing at such terrific speed that the cars sway an.i jump am:l.oe drivers themselves never expect to reach, home safely. Passengers and wayfarers near the line are alike in danger. For their part, the American people patronise indecent bicycle races, where not life, but intellect is in the balance. It is not for an outsider to fix the comparative criminality. of Government and people. It is perhaps sufficient to point out that more is expec- ted from a Government in the way of precept and example than from a people who follow the bent of their inclination. Americans may argue that the test of racing is the most practical and satis- factory way of awarding a contract in which speed is a special desideratum. But it panders to a taste for unhealthy sensationalism, of which America already has too much, and it possibly in- volves serious loss of life. No objection could well be more weighty.

Now that the Electric Lighting Committee of Warrington is in possession of the report of Mr. Preece on the subject of establishing an elec- trical supply undertaking in the Borough we hope that no time will be lost in coming to a decision. The appointment of Councillor Monks as chairman of the committee will no doubt give general satis- faction. He has displayed rare. business tact and ability as Chairman of the Sanitary Works Corn- rnittee, and the additional duty of piloting a large electrical scheme for the town will give him an Opportunity of adding to his laurels. Warrington has already lagged too much behind in the use of electricity for lighting and other pur- poses. There is, however, one compensation for this delay and that is that we shall have the benefit of the experience of other Corporations who have adopted electricity as an illuminant. The financial results so far as can b 3 gathered have been very satisfactory, and it is assuring to know that although electricity is a rival to gas, there are no case; where the two in- dustries have not flourished side by side.

The scheme recommended by Mr. Preece seems on the whole a very feasible one, and the estimate of £30,000 exclusive of buildings, very reasonable. Apart from the immense advantage of electricity for lighting purposes, the scheme will enable the Corporation to supply electricity for power pur- poses. If it can be obtained at a cheap rate small manufacturers will be quick to take advantage of it, and :there is every probability that the supply of electr:c power would prove even more remunera- tive than that of electric light. Mr. Preece has Pointed out that owing to the difficulty in obtain- ing early delivery of machinery, it is necessary to take immediate steps if the scheme is to be ready text winter—a matter which it is to be hoped will not be overlooked by the Electric Lighting .Committee.

On Satur- day night about 10 p.m. he assisted his mother-in-law to bed, and shortly afterwards his wife having occasion to go upstairs noticed her mother safe in bed. W.tness and his wife remained up to watch in the Now Year. On starting for bed about one o'clock on Sunday morning, witness an 1 his wife wen horrifiel to see (upon ooening the door which shut off the staircase), the body of Mrs. E lwards roll on to the floor at their feet. The body was stiff and cold. They sent for a doctor, and D. McDongall was soon in attendance. He pronounc life extincs.;.—Dr. Findlay McDougall testified to being called to the deceased. There wPra no marks of violence upon the body only two wounds, one on the side of the head and the other on the arm which he would assuim had been caused by the fall of the deceased. div.head: TWENTY STEP BRIDGE -MR. HEPITERD'S COMPLAINT.
div.p: TWENTY STEP BRIDGE -MR. HEPITERD'S COMPLAINT.

Re the bridge ever the Ship Canal Mr. James Hepherd of Stockton Heath wrote acknowledging copy of Mr. Put-s' letter with respect to this matter and said if it were as Mr. Potts stated all he could say was that it was only another example of how the loc d authorities let the Ship Canal Company put in any clauses they liked,- as if any private individual would take local pre- ceedinge. It he rememhere I correctly the Rural Council some time since threatened to summon the Ship Canal Company for the same offence ; if so why could not the County Council do so now, that was if they bad taken the read out of the hands of the Racal Council. In a later communication Mr. Hepherd said he had since had an opportunty of looking into the matter and he was under the impression that under Clauee 83 of the 1835 Ship Canal Act, the Daresbury Highway Board had power to recover penalties. Toe duties and powers of that Board were now vested in the Rural Council,and he must refer them to sub lection (10) section 83 of the Act a? 1885 under which he thought the Rural C ouncll should take the matter up against the Ship Canal Company'. If the matter was left t 3 private individuals to do so he was afraid the nuisance would be greater than ever. The Clerk to the County Council (Mr. R. Potts) wrote as follows :—le reply to your letter of yesterday's date, enclosing one from Mr. Ilepherd who has also written me on the subject. I was quite aware of section 83 to which he refers and the reason I did net recommend action being taken under it was that by sach secti ,n the Ship Canal Company are only required te work the bridges without unnecessary delay,and Questions would arise, and it would, I imagine,be difficult to prove that the bridee had been kept open au un-reasonable time whereas under section 88, which I apprehend applies to this bridge, as it is near Warrington, the Shp Canal Cemeany are prohibited under a penalty not exceeding £5 Wm keeping the bridge open for a longer period than 10 minutes. In the former case, however, the penalty is recoverable by the highway Board, or. now that the road leading up to the bridge is a Main road, by the County Council. while in the latter it is recover- able by the party aggrieved, and if,a3 I gather from Mr. Hepherd'e lett or to you he demurs taking proceedings himself, I will bring the matter utder till notice of the Main Roads Committee of this Council. I am writing Mr. Hepherd with a copy of this letter. The Chairman remark od it was now out of their hands for a time and anything further would come on after Mr. Pott's committee had dealt with the matter.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOAFD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOAFD.

The last tenting of the old Board was held on Tues- day night, under the presidency of Mr james Pritchari. Present ths Ray Canon Maitland Wool, Father Gore, Messrs F. J. Nrmu, J.P., E 'raison, C.C., J. IV. Lightburn (rl,rk). After a meeting of the mansgsment committee the business of the Board was proceeded with but tnere was nothing of public interest. It was de- cided to hold the first meeting of the now Board on Tuesday evening next. TIMMS TO CEUIRIVAN. _ _ _

Canon Wood proposed a very cordial vote of thanks to the chairman. During the three years Mr. Pritchard had held the post, he had been extremely attentive to his wo:k. and with his many occupations he must have found it diffi,ult to be so rezular and attentive in taking the chair. Mr. Frit hard had always shown a kindly disposition to them all. Mr. Imison seconded the rnition. As one of Mr. Plitchard's elder, colleagues he had always founi him exceedingly kind and courteous, and so he thought had all the members of the Board. Toe vote was accorled unanimously. _ _ .

Th Cha.rman, in reply, said th at i was satisfactory to find that the 1331r,i's returns of average attendance were so good ; far durinz the year ending September last the average atten lance was 84.'5, being the highest recorded. Since that date, however, in December the average had iecreased to 85 2. This showed that they were making proeress in this respect, and the fieures enmpared favourably with the averaze attendance is England and Wales. Beyond that they had to consider this question. They had in Runcorn a difficulty to deal with which did not occur to the same exteet in other He referred to the large class of canal lacat people which the Bard had to deal with, whose children probably only made ae average attendance of 3 halfdays per week, which brought dawn the averaee considerably. With regard to the Board's Schools they were in admirable working cond,- tion and during the last year they completed the exten- sion of Victoria-road Schools, which were now a magni- ficient pile of school buildings, which were a credit to the town and to the cause of education. The Board might also claim c-edit for working their schools in a re- enirkably cheap way. A short time ago, and probably ! the same thing prevailed to-day. the Runcorn School Board was worked at a less rate per head than any School Board Schools in England. This, he thought, spoke volumes for the Mosel. The Baud had also an excellent staff of teachers who had the confidence of toe Beard and he was sure they did their last in the educational interest of the children and had at heart their welfare. It was satis- factory to find this stat-i of efileiency as they closed their career. Every branch of their work was in a prosperous condition and in that state was it carried forward to their successors. On the proposition of the Chairman secon led by Father Gore a vote of thanks was passsel to the vice- chai rman, Mr. Imison.

ANNUAL TEA AND CONCERT AT THE SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE.
SUCCESSFUL YEAR'S WORK.

The large 1"03111 of the S3amen's Institute. Runclrn, presented a pl.sasin,z appearance, beLlecked with flags, bunting, and multi-coloured devices, on the occasion o: the annual tea party and concert, which was given to tne seamen and boatmen in the port of Runcorn, on Tuesday night. The proleedings commenced with a capitally served tea, at which over 200 sat down followed by a concert, and distribution of useful mailers, etc., with a" quid "of tobacco to each of the Eailors and boatmen who attended. The nae3tinz was eminently successful; and proved the value et the Seamen's Mission.

The concert was presided over by Mr. J. Meadowcrlft who was supported oa the platform by Mr3.Digges, Mrs Mead)wcroft, Mrs Lambert, the Rev. C R Uillck, N. J. Pole, Messrs. J. H. Hamilton, J. Stokes, and W. Saaw, missionary.

Mr. J. Meadowcroft said his first pleasure that evert- ing was to wish them all a very happy and prosperous new year. (Hear, hear.) According to the newspapers Runcora had behaved itself very credt ably,and he honed it would do so throughout the year just entered upon. The place he occupied that night was one that he had filled occwionally for the last twenty years. He believed he was a sort of old institution. When approached by Mr. Shaw, he exhibited some diffidence in accepting the post of honour feeling that they would be somewhat tired of an old figure, but Mr. Shaw had ultimately pre- vailed. Ile could truly say that his interest in the wel- fare of the Seamen's and Boatmen's Mission was as strong as ever it WIS upon its commence ment which was , a very loag period ago. As far as his individual efforts were concerned he hal d4ne all he could to assist Mr. Shaw in his work on be- half of the seamen in Runcorn. Mr. Shaw was one of those singular individuals who perhaps succeeded where few would succeed. Be had that amiable way about him that few could resist him—which was a most valu- able character in a missionary. The Institution was a most valuable one and not only looked after the interests of the seamen aed boatmen whiie they were in Runcorn, out he knew that Mr- Shaw spared no effort, no time, and even no expense in furthering their intere to else- where. (applause.) Toe speaker then instanced the thordughuesa of Mr. Shaw's work with illustrations o: the invaluable help he had afforded seamen, and paid him a high compiimeat. Toe traffic from Runco-n went to all parts of the sea, so that the boatmen's and sea- men's interests were ide utical. (Flear,hear.) Alluding to the improvement that was taking place in the trade of the port, Mr. Meaclowc-oft referred to the fact that the Runcorn "Lay-by" now afforded aceomo- ria,t'on to much larger vessels—some being of 3,300 and 3,500 to is burthen. Such vessels could never have come into Runcorn in the past and thus he felt, and Run- corn must feel, tat the need for toe Seamen's Mission was increasing rateer thaa diminishing. He would now ask Mt. Lambert (chaplain of the Mission) to say a few ' words about the mission te.fore the programme was proceeded with. (applause.) The Rev. E. Lambert, who was cordially received, said it was a very great pleasure to him as chaplain su- perintendent of the Mission to Come to Runcorn and find the Mission not only well supp-xted be the seamen bat also be such invaluable friends as the chairman and other ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Shaw was to be congratulated upon the bail of co-workers he had around him. (Hear, hear.) The value of the mission was manifest to the families of those unfortunate people who had lost their lives, through some untortun:te ac- cident. and althou4h the responsibility reted first with the Church neoplo of the fawn, he was glad to se so many of different persuasion rally round the flag and support the Institution. Tlvre was every hope of the Institution being supported in the future, an I he hoped that the sailors Would fl-ck to it not only on occasions when there was a good tea, a muffler, and a " quid of acca,".to be given Gut—(laughter)—but when there was spiritaal food to be obtained, and that which would serve them at all times. (Hear, hear.) He did not feel Trite such a stranger amongst them as upon pr:vious occasions, for had met many of them whilst they were lying windbaund in the " slough" when he went about in the mission launch " Good Cheer." The name of the vessel" Good Cheer" was dielinetive of the work of the Mission, and he extended to all a hearty welcome at all times to the good cheer the MiE• 9iOn provided not only at Runcorn, but at Birkeahea.d, Garston—sorne of them knew Mr. Thomas Williams there—(hear, hear),—Liverpool, and Ellesmere Port. They wanted the sailors to Ind religi'ms lives ; religion 7VII not at sottB rh'2,si;la 4u,v,ned cut of depth at 40 iath`inl4. For he knew' that men could be happy in the forecastle and in the cabin as anywhere else. W:th regard to the work at Runcorn. he would say they were a very good.mission,hut be would be a paor.super-

intendent if he said ill-7 were perfect, he would have to le ,vu them something that would encceirage them to be better. (Leuehter.) Whilst hiehly complimenting Mr. Shaw upon his work, he woeld say a word abut his band of workers. They were responsible for the success of the missioe as it was well known ole man weu'd not accomplish all by himself, and he hop .d they would con- tinue in su h a goad and generous work, and that the coining year would prove more su ice:sful than ever. (Loud applanse.) The GileirMaee. b Jere commencing the progiamme, said after suen an eloquent and f rcihle address it would be quite unnecessary for him to add another feature, but be would like to say a word about the Nor megian sailor. Mr. Shaw had a growing responsibility cast upon him by the increasi e nurnher of them sailors who came to Runcorn, tat; thou -.en there would he ril,nty to do with these foreigners, he was pleesed to be able to tost'fy to the respect which the Norwegians paid to rho observance of the Sunday. (Hear, hear.) The programme was then proceeded with. It was of a miscelianesus character and was well calculated to ap- peal to all. Tee first kern was a pianoforte solo by Miss Diggs who played with exquisite taste. " qieen of the Earth" by Mr. F. Shingier, was a crecli-ab'e per- formance, whilst the shirting of Mr. T. Woods was all that could be desired. The mandoline 'solo by Miss M. Dieges was skilfully executed, and in the second part of the programme the artiste gave a farther exhibition of her powers. Master Stanley Mead iwcroft (the son of the chairman), gave a pianoforte solo which was perfect i lin ts facile manipulation, but in the humorous and musieal sketch which he suusequently gare he showed evidence of a rare musical power that immediately made itself fe!* on the audience, who demanded an encore. Master John Rutter was likewise very successful in "Ship Britannia" which atifonce appealed to the nautical portion of the audience. The other items of the programme included "nome Deane Home "by Miss Coward ; a recitation, " The Lifeboat," by Mr. Oath- waite ; " One hundrei fathinme deep," by W. Johnson ; and a sweely rendered song" The cows are in the clover," by Miss Maggie Hill (a promising young local vocalist). Several encores were demanded. Mr. Shaw preposied a vote of thanks to the ladies and gentlemen who had subscribed the funds ; to the ladies who had presided at the tables' and to the entertainers. Fie rca :I the following telegram from Miss H. Hayes : " Royten, London. Hone everyone will thoroiighly eniev themselves to-night. Give all our best wishes for 1899." (Applause). The motion was seconded by Mr. Hamilton and carried unanimously. Mr. Dieges moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman, and referred to the great interest Mr. Meadowcroft took in the erection of the Institute and the work of the Mis- sion generally. The building cost £2,000 and Mr. Meadowcroft had lived to see that debt cleared off. (Hear, hear). Mr. Stokes seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously. The sailor's method ei,f conveying the votes of thanks was employed, and on the putting of each resolution the building rescunde 1 agoin with ringing cheers. The distribution of mufflers was made by Mrs Digges,

and Mrs. Meadowcrott d+stributed the to-ha:co, there being over 200 recipients. It may be stated that the warm mufflers are given by Miss El. Haves, and Miss Violet Hayes, of Frodiham, and they are knitted by the girls and boys of Frodsham, who work assiduously all the year round. Toe women and boatmen on the light- ships of the Upper Mersey Navigation, were not for gotten, as each individual was supplied with a Christ- mas box containing muffl ar, plum cake, oranges, and 'a quid "of tobarc which it is needless to say were fully appreciat:d. Tables were provided and preside over by the fol- lowing ladies :.—Mrs Lambut, Mrs Dicrer,es, Mrs Albert Able. Mrs Fred Able. Mn Johnson, Mrs G,orge Hewitt, Mrs Ciward, Mrs Price, Mrs Grounds, Mrs Somerfield, Mr Fred Swage, Miss Heasley, Miss C Abel, Miss Fisher and Miss Rosenberg, Weston. The decorations which were of an elabo-ate character were carried out by Mrs Evans, Miss Bowyer, Miss Coward, Mrs Cliffe, Mrs Tanks, and numerous assis tents.

LBY A CORItESPJNDENT Interesting reading will be found in the report of the Urban Council meeting of Thursday, particu- larly in tt, e award in connection with Riincorn Heath and Common. Of course, for a number of years the whole thing will be S 3 much " white- elephant" as is the case with the Widnes Park, but then it is a useful and necessary measure and clinches the townspeople's poAtion with regard to it for all time.

The utility of the Mereey Mission to Seamen has been forcibly brought before us by the recent tempestuous weather experiencd, and by the annual meeting held on Tate Adv. The Rev. C. K. Killick in supporting a vote of thanks touched upon the whole crux of the work of the Mission. He said "It embraced a branch of work that it would be utterly impossible for them (the clergy) to cover in connection with parochial work." So it dees,and therefore the gool folk of Itun:•,ora will sea it is deserving cf support. Another useful society, or mission, is the P.S.A., which has been held so successfully in connection with Bethesda Chapel for some time past. That als touches upon, or rather accomplishes work that no ordinary parochial work could comprehend, and it is pleasing to notice its increasing force and utility.

The last meeting of the School Board was held on Tuesday last, and the first meeting of the new one will be held next Tuesday. The ad tress given by Dir. James Pritchard (Was retiring chairmla of the Board) is an epitome of the work accomplished by the Bard during the year, and discloses nothing of an extraordinary nature,and what little there might be of interest meets with an indifferent recupion as it follows s 3 closely upon the School Board elec- tion.

Saturdly's match adds another two points to Runcorn's record at a welcome stage, and rosy hopes are entertained of further victories, and a conse- quent further addition in points.

The " gate " was not a large one, though per- haps the weather had somsthing to do with keep- ing people away. Yet, one thinks, a larger crowd is needed to maintain the old enthusiasm irk the club and its players. Runcorn has the talent. and with enthugastic Fupport might, as" Old Jack," puts it." improvoCso much as to secure the cup again."

The game deserves a remark or two. From start to finish there was a marked superiority in the Runcori fifteen, but of the two packs, TyMosley were far the best in the scrum. This, in face of the fact that latterly the Rancorn pack have been the bast part of the team is disappointing, and it is time the forwards looked to their laurels, or the backs will become their superiors—a thing we don't ware.;. What we do want is a " superiority all round ! A feature of the gams was the brilli- ancy of the passing of Runcorn. Shortly after half-past two en Menday afternoon, a horrible discovery was untie at Northwich. The dredger No. 2, ia charge of Captain Satton, was engaged in dreiging operations on the river Weaver, opposite the Crown and Anchor Hotel, when one of the buckets cer coming out of the waler was found to co3tain a human boly. Immediately the machleory was stopped and the police were informed of the gruesome find. The body is that of a well-developed man, supposed to be about 45 years of age, and the clothes denote that he was of the working &ASS% He was dressed in corduroys, with heavy nailed boots. Tao body was fearfully mutilated, being practically cut in two, whilst the trunk was badly torn. The face was cut very mech, this having evi- dently been done by the dredger or passing steamees. On Monday evening the body was identified as that of Martin Warl, of Warrington,who had been accustomed to travel from place to place with torashing machines. On Tires lay Mr. H C. Yatrs, the Cheihire coroner in- vestigated the c'rcumatancee attending the death of Martin Ward. It transpired that some three or four ' weeks ago deceased, who often fellowPd a threshing machine and worked between Northwich and Warring ton, spent a night at a Northwich lodging house, and then left with a man who had been acting as deputy at t lye lodging house. Th , latter returned the earn, night, but kit two days following an I was supp )vd to be in Manehester. div.head: I HAPPY NEW YEAR FOR RUNCORN.
div.p: I HAPPY NEW YEAR FOR RUNCORN.

The birth of 1899 was heralded in Runcorn, in keeping with the custom usually prevailing. On the eve of the New Year watchnight services were held in the numerous places of worship,all of which were well attended. Tne tolling of the Parish Church bell formed a fitting accompaniment to the passing of the last few moments of the old year. Then a clanging peal of the whole chimes within the tower proclaimel the birth of 1899, and a new year of promise was heralded. The distressing times through which the trade and commerce of Runcorn have been passing, may be said to have reached their zero in 1898, and with the advent of 1899 the tadespeople can confidently. , look forward te a steady advance—though natur- ally it will be slow enough for a time—in all round improvement. It, is to the Manchester Ship Canal that Runcorn attributes its rise or fall—that is the barometer by which the trade of Runcorn is regu- lated—and a glance in that direction at the present time indicates a marked rise. The turning point has been reached and shot over,and now the trades- man, tho artisan, and the property owner can con- fidently bustle about in preparation for the" good time coming." Another hopeful outlook is the development ob- servant in connection with the new industries that have been latterly started in the district, and we anderstand that the improved condition of things has come to stay, and that what migbt be called Op experimental stage is now pessod. Yet, although things are taking a bright turn, Runcorn will never become an ideal town, until the District Council really " tat " the prope ty owners a little more. That is" tax" them in the way of compelling them to prevent the deterioration of their property—" save them from themselves for" really some of the streets that exi it in the district are nothing more nor less than blocks of uninviting property with dilapidated fronts, broken windows, and filthy concomitants, which alone are sufficient to drive any would be tenant away. Again, some- thing might be done by having any structural alter- ations (such as shop fronts, etc.) carried out with a view to future all round improvement,and the lay- ing out of convenient and creditable streets. If this is borne in mind and acted upon, who knews but that the advent of tne next New Year will not only be a happier one but will come with a pleasanter retrcspect behind it.

div.p: CANON WOOD AND THE SCHOOL BOARD

The Rev. Canon Maitland Wood writes in the January numblr of the" Parish Magazine" :—" Mr. Stables and myseif have been assailed after a fashion as surprising as entirely unreaeonable, and we appreciate better than before the positioa of the Psalmist when he wrote I 14b Cur for peace, but when I speak unte them thereof they make them ready to battle: We do not believe for a mo:nent that we need enter upon a never-endine series of recriminatory speeches or letters ; if our lives and work in this place are not sufficient answer to our assailants no letters or speeches will suffice,but we think it enough to say once and fer all that we believe you know us well enough to estimate aright the value to be put upon all that has been said or printed. You know when the skin has been wounded it is a very good thing to cover over the raw place with an artificial skin or plaster until Nature has had time to form the new cuticle over the injured spot. Well, per- haps the true function of these letters and steries is to act the part of a plaster to the wounded feelings of the losers in this School Board contest, until the true skin of self-respect and kindliness shall have healed the wound and helped our friends the enemy to be our friends once more. Let us hone that this natural process will soon reach its completion. So much for us clergy ! but an attack delivered against our noble old parish schcols is another matter. Rumours appear to have circulated after the electim lee the effect tint, After the result of the poll reached the school Miss Sewell, the head- tress of the girls' school, announced it to till children, expressed her pleasure that the Church hai won, called for a show of hands, firstly of church children and secondly of chapel children, ard asked the latter if they were not sorry to be Chapel children.: I take the words from the postcript of a letter which Sir John T. Brunner caused to be printed and sent round Rancern. Perhaps as Sir I. T. Brunner represents. me, and a goed many who think with me .on ecticational matters in Parlia- ment, he will not think a suggestion from me an impert- inence. It is only tills —That it is never the part of a wise man to let himself zo or give his pen or tongue hump co say all it Irk-s before making inquiry. Fish- ing for grievances is an amusing and eometims even profitable occupation but it is well to catch a fish before you pepper him, and salt him, cut him open and fry him." "IThe Managers" says Caner' Wood, " finally felt that in the face of MiS3 Woodward's stead- fast declaration and her unblemished character they could not consider the story proved. It was made as clear as the day that Nonconformists' children were not and never had been subjected to any unfairness or un- kindness, and that the children themselves had not on the occasion itself, been annoyed in any way, in short it became evident that the whet() m4t'er was of the most trivial character, end that the holding of the inquiry was itself like cracking a nut with a steam-hatraie.r. However, the nut was cracked,and there was nothing an it. The only pity is that anyone should have thought it worth while to fan so small a matter into a blaze, and that little girls of ten shou'd have been induced to sign written out statements without the consent of the par- ents. Ido not believe that any harm has been none to our mucteloved parish scheols, nor to the cause of the i Voluntary sohools in general, which s dear to this t3wn of Runcorn and to me."

div.head: MESSRS. Cao WIELD'S WORKS. PUBLIC INSPECTION,
div.p: MESSRS. Cao WIELD'S WORKS. PUBLIC INSPECTION,

Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons Limited threw open their works for public inspection last Thursday and Friday and the general response to the in- vitations was evidence of the fact tnat the privilege was. appreciated. Considerably more than 8,00 persons responded to the invitations, and the re- sources of the firm were somewhat taxed to enable the visitors to make a detour of the premises in comfort. But like other difficulties which the firm have been obliged to face this was serrnounted and the affair passed off satisfactorily. The inspection is the outcome of a happy idea of the young women employed by the firm wao, about twelve months ago, asked permission of Dr. Markel, the managing director, to allow their parents and friends to visit the works, and thus be able to see for themselves the favourable conditions under which they laboured. The request was readily acceded to, and proved such a success that this year it was decided to extend the invitation to others. Entering the box room, the visitor was intro- duced to the noise inseperable from the making of boxes. The labour attached to this work has been reduced to a minimum by the use of ingeniously devised machinery and the rapidity with which the boxes are knocked together is remarkable; in fact a box seems to be made in less time than that occu- pied by a joiner in lifting his hammer. in the same pltice some interesting rotary mechinery is at work printing on wood from a brass fount. This kind of printing is to be seen on all Messrs. Crosfield's boxes. Passing on to the stamping room, boys and girls are to be seen working harmoniously together, putting the finishing touches to the soap betere it reaches the hands of the purchaser. The soap sans are the next objects of interest. Two of them are each capable of containing 160 tons of saponaceous material, and a printed card informs the visitor that. they are the largest pans in the world. After a brief survey of the dry soap room the visitor reaches the cheap toilet department, where the familiar penny tablets are to be seen in groat variety. The printing and lithographing rooms were also thrown open for inspection, but perhape the most interesting, and cer- tainly the most attractive-looking room is that known as the milling room. Here the best toilet soaps are made, and packed in dainty boxes by a lerge number of gies with smiling faces and nimble fingers, who chatted freely over their work and seemed to enjoy it immensely. This depart- ment has only been in existence about two years, but already it is rivalling with the best toilet houses in the Kingdom. At the preseat time the firm are selling about 20 tons a week of the teighes class of toilet soap. such as the Peerless Erasmic, and the" De Luxe." The most recent addition to the firm's numerous departments is the manufac- ture of scent. The " Erasmic " scent wee placed upon the market two months age, and the demand for it has been so great that the firm have been un- Ole to adequately cope wiqi it. The department occupies a portion of the milling room, and R number of girls were to be seen busily engaged in labelling bottles, and preparing them for the market. A striee eye is kept on the department by the Excise Officer, who has an office on the premises. in the stores, samples were shown of Messrs. Crosfield's productions. These number about 300 different specialities, and additions are continually being made. The last place to be looked at wes the jewellery rootn.Thia department has been in existence about eighte=n months, but it has only recently been removed to Warrington from London. It is the outcome of the awards which are given to purchasers of " Rainbow " soap, the value of the award depending upon the number of wrappers re- turned. Mr. T. Mitchell superintends this depart- ment, and he displays all the resourcefulness of a ;jeweller in desc-ibing the splendid time-keepers, cruets, and jewellery of every description in his charge. And then one is inclined to ask,who wonld be without a watch when you can get one for 300 soap wrappers? The inspection of the works cannot do other than favourably impress the visitor with the high busi- ness qualities displayed by the firm and the good relations which seem to exist between the em- ployers and the workpeople. It is such visits as these which will di-pel the sinister, and absolutely false rumours which are sometimes circulated. Great changes have, of course, been made within the lest five years. Old methods have had to give place to new, .and perhaps not without; a little friction. But that the efforts put forth have been justified is shown by the manner in which the firm has gone ahead within recent yea's. There is a strong determination on the part of the firm to stand in the front rank in their line of busi- ness, and that they are succeeding is beyond ques- tion. At the present time the firm employ at War- rington, Liverpool and depots in various parts of the kingdom about 2,000 workpeople. Seeing that the progress of the firm is cencomitant with that ef Warrington the firm should have many well wishers in the town, and it, is to be hoped that the present condition of the firm is but the beginning of sill better things.

div.head: WEATHER. SEASONABLE REFLECTIONS BY A SUFFERER.
div.p: THE WEATHER. SEASONABLE REFLECTIONS BY A SUFFERER.

As no one seeirs inclined to take the initiative and subject the Clerk of the Weather to a little gentle criticism, I have decided to do el myself. In coming to such a decision,l have been prompted by the apathy displayed by the bulk of the people. and, too, I feel, in a measure encouraged in my purpose, by the fact that 'shill be voicing or wording a popular sentiment, and that whatever I say in a recriminatory sense wilt be supported by nearly the entire population of the North of Eng- land.

Ccitidsm is a beautiful thing; and, practically it governs every matter nowadays,from boxing and football, to poetry and politizs. Your true critic of a given subject is the rain who,out of a vast and intimate knowledge,can praise perfection and ques tion weakness, so that, on behalf of the interested public, only the good and the best of a thing shall live.

I mention my standard of criticism, jut to justify theee,my opinions and myself, as the writer, in the action lam taking. I claim the right to criticise the Clerk of the Wea.ther;and.it need be,to condemn his judgment in carrying out the duties entailed by his office of weather providing, because I have an intimate knowledge of what is good and what is not good weather. I .go out everyday and I went to Blackpool recently. I did not like the weather even there. As one man's dislige orlike of any given thing is often a question of taste and,equally often, unreliable and egotistical; so I did not pin myself, at, Blackpool, to my own judgment. There were fifty thousand other people in the town and they had arrived in special trains from dreary places to disport themselves by the sea in the suulight and to enjoy the healthy air. Instead, they were Cooped up in palaces of amusement or public- houses, aria every time the woman looked outside they said " Bother " ; while the men, glancing through the doors, said a variety of words, all well chosen, tersely forcible, bat, alas wholly un- printable. The weak point la the Weather Clerk's programme this yell 'iss been hie bad taste in catering, on public holidays, for the democracy. Public holidays were specially made for the workers. They are a fine institution in their way, but there is n t enough of them. Ido not wish to ;sander tile gallery; but, personally, ,I do beaeve Vest soy happiness would be enhanced if a worlting week consisted of six holidays. Yet holi- days are of no use unless there is fine weather pre- vailing, except to publicans and theatre proprietors. Da not run away with the idea that I am insinuat- ing that the Clerk of the Weather has been "got at" by the two necessary catering classes I neen- don. I would not insinuate so much; but, as there is such a preponderance of evidence, I am , prepare,' to think it. You cannot get across with the libel laws if you only think; it is the talking and writing that make the trouble. The workers are in the majority in this world ; yet, w)-die they are in the majority, they get the least number of holidays. Therefore—a fair logical conclusion—when they have a holiday the Clerk of the Weather should make all barometers point to "set fine; "and- at the same time he should see that- every one speaks the truth. What has this Clerk of the Weather done, only this year? Take Easter Monday for instance. On that day it rained with a persistency so striking that one coul4 bear the sound caused by the impact as it struck the people. I went to Blackpool that day, too ; and, along with some thousands of fellow mourners, lamented-inwardly with much bitterness. Still officials are not. infallible and I decided that the Clerk had made a mistake; that, in short, he had erred in ignorance. Going home, with twenty damp trippers huddled together in one carriage, we exchanged experiences. Strange to say. though We had been strangely tried, we were not bitter, in fact, a genial soul from Oldham voiced our senti- ments when he said: "Happen it 'ull be bet-ter next Whissun."

ThisWhirmintide Monday was:—A deluge of rain, a desert of falling water with not a dry oasis; a free shower bath for a whole county, minue towels; an incentive, tempting a frail people to sin, by blasphemy, throughout a day ; a dreary visitation, worse than an eerie nightmare, born of muffins or a parcake supper; a day worse than two of the forty which were once devoted to ilioling the world ; a holi'l ly which was not a holiday, but a lingering punishment that sowed the seeds for a crop of su;cides.

_ The Clerk who arranged the weather programme for the twO holidays ought to be sent to golden Klondike clad only in a suit of p‘ jamas, and with no provisions; or failing that, he might be con- demned to spend a week. under the weather condi- tions he has just arranged, in a volunteer encamp- ment.

I could say a lot more, I could deprecate a pro- gramme which has embodied the ideas: That winter is summer, that spring is autumn, and that it is better to have a chaotic mass of pimbled seasons with their atmospheric characteristics all clashing, than au orderly succession and reasonable conditions. _ _ _ _ - .

Instead I will express a wish that my little critic- ism, not unduly spiteful, may have a chastening effect; that the Clerk of the Weather shall revise his programme and that the process of democratic evolution which is now taking place may reach him, too, sal teach him to have a certain amount of regard for that fitness of things which is rightly deemed eternal, Warrington GEORGE EDGAR.

div.head: ELECTRIC LIGHTING OF WARRINGTON. REPORT BY MILA. H. PREECE
div.p: THE ELECTRIC LIGHTING OF WARRINGTON. REPORT BY MILA. H. PREECE

The Electric Lighting Committee have received the report and scheme for establishing an elel- tricity supply undertaking in the Borough from Mr. A. H. Preece. A.M.1.C.E., of Westminster, Lon- dma The report is of a private and confidential cbaracttr, but there are certain points which may with advantage be made public.

CONTINUED PROGRESS OF ELECTRIC LIGHTING. There are now over 80 local authorities, Mr. Preece points out, supplying electricity in their districts. Over 25 works are in progress,and many more are about to start. In the provinces alone out or a total of 2,000,003 lamps connected to supply stations over 1,50,000 are served by municipal works. The total capital invested in municipal works exceeds £4,000,600 and the Local t3overnment Board are continually holding enquiries for further loans for new works and for extensions, it is in- teresting also to find numerous authorities negotia- ting, awl, when possible, purchasinv the successful undertakings recently established by companies in their districts. Such towns as Liverpool, Sheffield, Birmingham, Hastings, have had to pay very large premiums to obtain that which they thoughtlessly gave away a few years ago.

div.head: SCHEME SUGGESTED.
div.p: THE SCHEME SUGGESTED.

Proceeding to define his scheme for Warringt6n Mr. Preece remarks that the compulsory area in- cludes the following streets :—Bridge-street, Bold street, Sankey-street, Palmyra-square, Wilson Pat- ten-street, and Horsernarket-street. This is only a small portion of the Borough, but in it are in- cluded many of the principal public buildings and shops. It was extremely difficult to estimate the probable demand in this area,but in his opinion the first plant should be large enough to supply not less than 10,000 eight candle power or 5,003 sixteen candle power lamps burning at one time, or 12,500 eight candle power lamps fixed in consumers pre- mises. In nearly every town it had been necessary to consider extensions before the plant had been in working order six months. In many cases the first plant had afterwards proved small and hence un- economical. It was not wise to have engines and dynamos of small sizes. The plant proposed would always be economical, however large the installa- tion might become. The improved lighting of some of the streets gave everyone an interest in the un- dertaking. It was of advantage to all who used the streets, and it acted as a good advertisement to the industry. Hence he suggested that arc lamps, which gave a brilliant light, should be fixed about 70 yards apart in such streets as Bridize-street,San- key-street, and liorsemarket-street. The lighting would be increased at least five times, and the cost would not be very much above the present cost. The scheme recommended as a start would therefore consist of a plant for 12,500 lamps, including 20 arc lamps in the streets. Adequate mains would also be provided in all the compulsory streets, with plenty of spare pipes for drawing in new feeders.

div.head: BITE
div.p: THE BITE

Referring to the site for the electrical w.,rks Mr.Preece states that the Fite in the old Gas Works is in every way suitable for the undertaking. It is c-ntral and there is plenty of room. The plans submitt.d with the report show the extent of the buildings and the proposed ar- rancremc,nt of the generating plant. There was space for at least 5,000 horse Power. Thus the ultimate plant could supply 100,000 8 c.-p.latnps avid 1,000 horse power for electric tramways. It was impcosible to say what W.irrington would he evl,n ten years hence, but it was doubtful whether it would require so much power by then. If it did so the Electric Lighting Committee would be fully justified in requisitioning further portions of the site, which were now given ta other purposes.
THE SYSTEM.

The question of system Mr. Pzezce says, is generally determined by the site. The central position of the old Gas Works enabled him to recom mend the l.w pressure three wire system. This E. ystem was of sufficient adap- tability, now that 440 vclts was permitted, to reach points over 11 miles away. It also allowed the use of accumulators to store electr;city and supply all the energy required after midnight. The pressure was suit- able for tramways, so that the engiws all dynamos could be used t.) generate electricity for lighting pur- pos,s and tor the tramways.
THE ESTIMATED COST.
Mr. PREECE proceeds to give a dtailed statement of

the estimated capital expenditure ineurrel in erecting nlant and laying mains, el-c. for an estimated demand of 12,500 eighl; candle power lamps. Ho estimates the total cost of the scheme as shown on the drawings, but ex- clusive of the buildings, as follows :—maohinervonains, etc., £24,6oo;thstruc-.ors and platform £3.1.00; envireer- inc.; and contingencies, £2,300, total £30,000. Mr.'Pretc after giving a brief description of the propos'.-A arrange- ment of the works, gives a carefully preriared estimate of the probable finaniiial result, and from comparative statements of the cost of working in other towns is able to show that assuming the output at the low figure of 170,000 units there would be a profit after paying work- ing expenses and '..nt rest and sinking fund. He states that he has taken no credit for the destruction of the refuse, nor for the probable saving on coal. He had not the least doubt that a considerable benefit would be obtained from the combination.

div.head: ITS POSSIBILITIES.
div.p: ITS POSSIBILITIES.

Mr. Preece further points out that the streets in the compulsory area contain many insportant buildings and places of bu,ioess ; while many others are quite close to the compulsory area, which may be reachel without difficulty or great expense. The total of 10,000 lamps should be easily obtained in twelve months after start- ing. In aldition to the demand from private consumers for electricity for lighting, there was the supply of electricity for power purposes. In Warrington there were numerous factories, and if power was supplied at a cheap rate it was certain to be largely adopted, espezially by the smaller firms. An electric motor was clean. It was easily placed directly on the spot where power was required. It could 131 adapted to any speed or gearing. It also did not require the same attention as as engine and a boiler, or even a gas engine. There was a large gain in being able to turn the power on and off at a moment's notice, without causing

waste of energy and consNuent waste of money. The generating works had also been specially arianged with a view to supplying electricity to tramways. The lighting load was never required more than two or three hours per day at its maximum, and hence there is only a very short time available for the earning of the neces- sary profits. When electric tramways were supplied the staff and the plant were fully utilised, and everything was worked at its maximum efficiency for some hours every day. The result was that electricity could be produced at less than half the cost when only a lighting load was sunpli,d. He recommended the comrnitt3 to take immediate stens to carry out a scheme, at an esti- mated cost of £3o,ooo,exclusive of the buildings. The scheme to be so arranged that power might he supplied to private consumers and, when necessary, to electric tramways. Ile recommended that two refuse destruc- tors should be erected in connection with the boilers for the generating plant, in order that the waste heat pro- duced by the destructor of the town refuse might be utilised as much as possible. A cheap supply of elec- tricity would bring electric light and electric power within the reach of everyone, and the conditions of working in all places of business would be immensely improved. Financial success was assured, and he felt convinced that the undertaking would prove in every way of immense benefit to Warrington.

AN OLD STORY.--The well-known humorist, Alphonse Karr, who owned an estate in the southern part of France, had for a neighbour an elderly Italian count, whose library was exceed- ingly well stocked and was considered a sight well worth seeing in that 'locality. One day. the witty author, who had not yet met his neighbour, sent his servant with a card to him, requesting the loan of a certain book. The eouut replied in a very p6lite note that he was extremely sorry that he could nut oblige Mr. .E.1.7r, hut that it V; C. 3 with him a matter of principle never to land any baoks for use outside of his own library. At the same time he invited his neigh- bour to came to his house at any time, and hie library would be at Mr. Karr's 'disposal all day. Karr, who. was anxious to obtain certain information, went to the count's house and made, notes Irons the particular book in the library that he wanted.- A snort time afterwards the count needed a sprinkler, and sent to his literary neigh- bour, asking ior tire loan of cue. Karr, who had not forgotten the way in which his request for a. book had been answered, now sent to thc caunt an extremely polite note, couched in the following terms :—" I deeply regret the impossibility of obliging you by tue loan of a sprinkler; but, as a matter of principle, I could not possibly allow my sprinkler to be used outside Of my garden; but if you desire to use it on my own lawn, I shall gladly place the opriakier at your disposal all day.'" VEDA' HARD Lt7CRl.—" Speaking of hard luck-," said a commercial who travelled tor a piano firm, "I believe I can gi vu you a story that's just a little bit worse than you've heard." Of course no one believed him, but it was known that he had a good imagination, so he was told to go ahead. "Someone who was fond of a joke steered me against a morose old farmer," he explained, "and I undertook to sell him a piano. I had got pretty well warmed up to my subject before I learned that he was a bachelor, who lived all alone on his farm, and that the whole thing was intended as a joke on me. I would have given up then is he had not held out a little hope. "'Friend,' ho said, . 'the trouble with me is that I ain't got no one to play a piano. If you'll get me someone to play it--' "'A wife, for instance?' I suggested. He intimated pretty strongly in answer to that suggestions that any self-respecting man with a wife ought to have a piano, and that he would get one mighty quick in those circumstances." " I know the story, broke in one of the listeners. "I've heard it before. Just to show practical jokers what you could do, you went out and found a wife for him." "That's what I did," admitted the agent, " Well, you'd better get a new story. Every sewing-machine agent in the country is tell. big this one, just to show what a fine salesman he is.' "I guess they're not telling this one," retorted the agent. "I guess they are; I've heard it." "Then finish it." " Why, got him the wife, and sold him the,piano." "No, I got him a wife, and found too late that she already had a piano, and on the stength of that he declined to but another. That's why I speak of it as hard luck."

div.head: COUNCILLOR F R. ROBERTS AND SOCIALISM.
div.p: COUNCILLOR F R. ROBERTS AND SOCIALISM.

Sir,—Mr. Roberts stated a': Mr. Walelron'a meeting that" Socialism was Coercion." He now denies this, but admits saying " lam no Socialist for the root principle of Socialism is Coercion." Then he goes on to say" that he one.ht perhaps to have said that ite practical application implies Coercion and that of the most unmerciful kind." It seems Mr. Roberts does not know his own mind, or else, is very careless in his use of words. He also pro- ceeds to infer or insinuate t'-at (.1) Socialists would make frse with other people's property? (2) that Socialism is a Superstition. In trying to explain his remark Mr. Roberts hai made his case worse. The I.L.P. again characterise these statements as false and misleadingand renew tbe challenge to either a public debate or discus- sion. If Mr. Robertsje afraid he will have to pay any money, let him rest content, for the will nay the rent of a room and advertise the meeting. M.. Roberts has a 9erfect right to " express an honest opinion "bat the statement in question was an assertion and an ac- cusation made at a public meeting without any attempt to justify the remark. He ought to be prepared to give reasons for such a public statement or else expect severe criticis:n. Yours, etc., THE WARRINGTON, I.L.P.

Sir,—As one present at Mr.Waldroa's lecture, I should !ike to say a few words in the present discussion. My impression of Mr. Roberts's remark re Coercion, was similar to " Fairnlay's "—bal English as it was— although Mr. Roberts now denies it. it was made in what I thought a reckless manner at the close of Mr. Waldron's address, and it seemed a rather unkind " cut" at Mr. Waldron,for in his speech,he went so far on Socialist lines that every Socialist present could heartily applaud. In fact with the exception of the ridiculous caricature of Socialism Mr. Waldron drew from a French writer, unknown to me, and unnamed by Mr. Waldron, the Socialists must have agreed with hina. His remarks on home life, environment of the people,— particularly the condition of the children, and the ques- tien of true individuality, freedom, liberty, and the whole-hearted way he declared himself a land nationatizer with the correlative Nationalization of Mines and Railways, he might have been a Socialist lecturer on a Socialist platform. As reglr is the" net very preound questions " put at The close of the lecture, Mr. Waldron found them inter- esting, for in a gentlemanly and courteous manner he replied at considerable length ; and it is wortlsy of note, that he confessed to "going the whole of the way" with a question containing the very essentials of Socialism as tanght in England to-day, viz, collemive control and ownershin of the land and instruments of production. As to Mr. Roberts' statement of a" decided pause" after Mr. Waldron answered the third queition. I must disagree with him, for a person who was near to me was rising when the chairman, hurriedly as I thought,closed the meeting. Anyhow it seems to me it was the chair- man's duty to ask ii there were any other questions. It is perfectly true that Socialists are always ready fur dis- cussion—different to some of their opponents,who appear

afraid. There is one inconsistency in Mr. Roberts's let er. He says he does not intend to discuss the question. and just a little later proceeds to ask three questions. This is the way to commence discussion. It is hardly in the scope of this letter to attempt a reply. but it appears to me that: lst.Socialists point out the evils of land monopoly, teach the people what conditions should prevail, and show thenu two or thve ways in which a 89111 ion of the land question may be found. They have no" cut aa dried scheme" but are glad to receive knowledge and truth from any source. And, Mr. Editor,they can trust the people when the time is ripe for action. This ques- tion is rapidly corning to the front. 2nd: Mr. Roberts does not rem to know the difference between Socialism and Communism. He must be thinking of the early Christian church of which we are told "They had all things in common." Perhaps Mr.Reberts will tell us how far the Christian church to-day has improved on the ethical conditions of that early Christian Society ? 3rd. To mention the name of Christ as presumably ap- proving modern society is opposed to anything like reason. Imagine the teacher of the "Fatherhood of God and Brotherhood of man" supporting a land system whereby a comparatively fee, individuals hold and control, that, without which, people can not live; and extort from thore who labour on the land a mass of wealth, enabling the holders to live in luxury and idle- ness ; where al forms of capital are used in the pro- duction of goods,not for the satisfaction of public needs, but in order to get as much money—profit and interest —as possible. Imagine Christ supporting a system which allows men to get "rich " oa the labour of little children. A system which forces neighbours to engage In a" sub throat competition" :n business six days a week after which, on the other day, they profess in church to be" Brothers in Christ." _ A system based on

the intensely selft3h principle of " Buy in the cheapest market and sell in the dearest " ; the whole dominates by the pernicious doctrine of" every man for himself." Is this Christianity ? Nay. Christ's lite, teaching and example condemns the present system and it behoves the Christian Church—who profess discipleship—to attempt at once to put into practical operation the principles of their Mastcr.—Yours SOCLILIST.

A COIIRECTION.

We are informed that the person in charge of the jewellery depart-nent at Messrs. Crosfield's works is Mr. F. Gleave and not Mr. T. Mitchell as stated in our last issue. LECTI:TRE IN THE CHRISTADELPHIAN ROOM.

On Sunday evening at the Chtistadelphian Room, 80ld-street, a course of lectures was commenced, the speaker being Mr. W. J. Young, of Chester, who took for his subject, "Does it matter what we be- lieve? The Word of God contrasted with popular Tit:3M." Mr. Young in the course of an interesting lecture dealt with the various kinds of belief, par- ticularly mentioning the two extremes —Trinitarian and Unitarian. PRESENTATION TO MR. STEPFIEN DALE,

The most interesting item i 4 the proceedings of the annual congregational tea meeting and enter- tainment, held on Monday evening, in connection with the Independent Methodist Brick-street Mis- sion was the presentation of an electro plate tea and coffee service to Mr. Stephen Dale by the mem- bers,congregation, and scholars of the above church and school. The president of the church, Mr. Thomas Mayhall, made the presentation, and in a few well chosen remarks commented on the excel- lent services the recipient of the pres3nt had ren- dered to the church. The inscription on the tray was as follows: "Presented to Stephen Dale, Esq.' by the members of the Independent Methodist Brick Street Mission, as an acknowledgment of his gratuitous services as architect and supervisor of the New Building, January 2nd, 1899." On receiving the gift Mr. Dale, who was heartily and repeatedly applauded said he had taken it as a duty in giving his services in co-operation with the self-sacrificing efforts of the members of Brick Street Mission in the erection of the new . mission hall. Ile hoped that goad work might be wrought in the locality in which it was built, and expressed his thanks to all those who had subscribed to the present he had received, stating that it would be very much prized by himself and family. There was a large attendance at tea, and the entertainment which was very attractive and provided much mirth, was presided over by Mr. Thomas Mayhall. Mr. A. Grounds with his usual ability gave his laughable sketch "The Village Concert," and in response to an encore he favoured the audience with musical selections on his Gramophone. lie also gave his ventriloquial entertainment which was thoroughly enjoyed. Miss Elizabeth Lawton sang with much effect two solos entitled "The Children's Borne" and" Dada." Two solos" Ever of thee I'm fondly dreaming" and "My pretty Jane," were well rendered by" Mr. henry Lightfoot, and Messrs. William Barton and Henry Lightfoot sang a duett entitled "Laughter." The risibilities of the audience were aroused by an amusing negro sketch entitled "Lodgings to Let," which created plenty of fun,the various characters acquitting themselves creditably. During the evening the secretaries of the. Church and Sunday School gave their annual reports. On Tuesday evening the scholars tea meeting was held. There was a large number present. After tea, the officers and teachers catered for the children's en- joyment, games and racing were indulged in which gave much pleasure. On Sunday over 90 book prizes were presented to the scholars in the Sunday school for regular and punctual attendance during the past year.

div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
P.S.A.

At the usual weekly meeting of the above held on Sunday, there was oaly a mxlerate attendance. Mr. G. Clark presided, and a capital address was given by Mr. G. Dring. Vocal selections were given by Mr. S. Dring, and Mr. B. Latimer gave selections on the violoncello. Mrs. Litiraer presided at the piano. SEVERB WELTURR AT EARLBEITOWIC_

On Monday night a strong gale blew over Earles- town and Newton.accompanied by a deluge of rain. Fortunately, however, no damage was done to property, beyond the dislodging of a few slates. In Cross-lane a large tree in the front garden of Mr. 3. Barr, was uprooted, and thrown into the road, breaking the garden palings, and blocking the road against vehicles. Fortunately no one was in- jured by the falling of the tree. PoLlon CISRS.

At the Newton Town Hall on Monday morning. before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie and C. B. F. Borron, Thomas 'levity, a boiler maker of St. Helens, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the Railway Sta.tion at Eartestown, and also with assaulting one of the porters. named Job Church, on Saturday night. tie was fined 23. 61. and costs for being drunk. and 5s for the assault.—John Flaherty, of Riarlestown, and John Dillon, for being drunk and disorderly on the Ist inst., were each fined 23. 61. and CMCS.—P.O.'s Gathercale and Gascoigni proved the cases. NEW YEAR'S HOLIDAY AT EA.RLESTOWI.

_ The fact of New Year's Day falling on Sunday had a somewhat restraining effect upon the bois- terous spirits in the time-honoured custom of" let- ting in" the New Year. There were many people about the streets until a vary late hour, and the various places of worship where watch-night ser- vices were held, were largely attended. Fortun- ately the weather was fine and thus people were able to move about without inconvenience, and the police had no trouble with any roystering spirits. Monday was observed as a general holiday by all the tradespeople, and by all the works, with the exc?ption of the Viaduct, which re-opened after being closed a week. The weather, however, was of a dreadful character, and many had, perforce, to remain indoors. A football match was arranged between Earlestown and Astley Bridge, but in con- sequence of the stormy state of the elements, it had to be abandoned when only half through. At night a terrific gale raged, and the streets were deserted.

SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A. S. HELENS WOMAN.

On Tutsday afternoon, Elith Craig, wife of a cab driver, reiidiog at 120, Crab-street, St. Helens, commi•- ted suicide in a most determined manner. SiFI was found in the kitchen with her thr3at badly gashed, and a blood-stained table knife close by. Dr. Do w was im- mediately called in,but the woman expired in the curse of a few minutes. THE DROWNING MYSTERf.

Mr. S. Brighouse, clunty coroner, held an inquest at St. Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday, on the body of William Key, 36 years old, lab urer. of Parr-street, who was found drowned in the canal at Pocket Nook on Wm- day afternoon. It appeared that deceased was drunk on New Year's Day,hut went to his work on the night turn at Pocket Nook Glassworks. Later on he left the works to visit a beerhouse on the opposite side of the canal, which he had to cross by a bridge. He left the beeraouse to gs back to his work, bat he was not again seen until his body was found in the canal on the f 0110 wing day.— James Forber said he heard cries coming from the direc- tion of the canal on Sunday night, and they got lights and made a search, but could see no one in tim water. —Constable Whalley spoke to the recovery of the body. Deceased still held his pip 3 in the &leen of his left, hand.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned."

div.p: - ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
EA.RLESTOWN ROVERS v. NEWTON &THLE rm.

These local rivals met for the first time in a League encounter on the Mesnes ground on Sat'arday. The teams were very evenly matched and promo-, to time Mr. T. Lvtlogoe (the President of the Rovers Club) kicked off for the Athletic. Rhuebetham and Ellis im- mediately made great headway on the left and Rhue- botham dribbled finely into the goalmouth, and when within about 20 yards of the Athletic goal ho le*:, fly g:ving the custodian no chance whtteYer. This early success seemed to put fresh We into the Rovers and they again took up the running, the result of some flue com- bination being that Ellis snored the Rovers' second goal two minutes after the restart. R-aised by these two early revorses, the Athletics made strenuous efforts to reduce the le-td but the Rovers bteks held them well in check and frustrated all their attempts at scoring. At this point of the game Chadwick and Lowe had a-lively discussion which eventually led up to fighting,for which both players were ordered off the field. Play now 1)3- came very rough up to the interval when the score stood Rovers, 2; Athletics 0. Upon nsuming tee Athletics were seen to better advantage. A fine run on the left by Broster b?ing nullified by Hamilton tagging his centre high over toe bar. Still undaunted the Athletics again returned to the attack and they kept up a hot fusilade on the Rovers goal the ball being eventually shot into the net through a host of players. Encouraged by this the Athletics tried hard to draw level and it took the Rovers defence all their time to keep them out. This hey managed to do, however, and the whistle blew with the score :—Eirlest3wa Rovers, 2 ; Newton Athle- tic, 1.

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT EARLESTOWN.

At Newton Town Hal on Monday morning before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie and C. B. F. Barron James String- fallow, (23), of William-itreet. Gorton and late of Earles- town, an iron turner, was brouzht up on a charge or. at- tempting to commit suicide by drowning in the Sankey Canal near Bradlegh Bridge, Earlestown. He was re- manded to the County Seesions at Warrington. On Wednesday he was similarly charged at Warrin;- ton.—Fre let ick Collin,labourer, 41,Eng,ine-road ,Nowton, said on the thy in question he was walking along te Sankey Canal near Bradlegh Bridge and when about 300 yards away saw defendant take his jacket off ant 3 jump in the water. Witness asked him what he wanted to do, and defendant replied that he waivel to do away with himself as he had no home. Witness tcok him to Junc- tion-lane and gave him up to James McGovan who handed him over to the police.—P.C. Aspen said when he received the prisoner in cuEt ody his clothing was wet and when he charged him with attempting to commit Isuicide prisoner made no reply.—Mrs. Stringfellow mother of the prisoner said he lived with her at home but 'he had been drinking all the Christmas holidays. He did not take much as a rule. His father was living. Pthoner was an iron-turner and gave her about 12. a week.—ln answer to the Bench Stringfe!low said if he had been in his sober senses he would never have done such a thing. He only remembered getting out of the water.—The bench bound prisoner to come up for judg- ment when called upon and discharged him on the mother promising to look after him.
