The first ()F. the meetings in the campaign of Colonel Richard Pilkinet on in connection with his cenlidature for toe Newton Division was held in the Town Hall, Eerleetown, on Wednesday evening. There was a fair attendaace. Mr. C. B. F. B orron presided, and he was supported on the platform by Captain J. F. Begot, M.P. (Kendal), Colonel R. Pilkington, Messrs. T. D. Gricuke Drayton, R. Slone, H. J. Longton, W HollandeOwen, T J. Gillespie, W. Walton, W. TtloM3ol, W. Collingwood, R. Barton, J. H. Forster, Dr Handyside, Dr Patterson. Toe Chairman said he hid received several letters of apology for noa-at-eadance, but he did not think it ne- cessary to real them. After paying a complimentary tribute to the late Member, who, he said, had served for 12 years and had earned their respect aad esteem, Lord Newton had now been, moved to the House of Lord, and he was sure he was only eat:ming their feelings when he expressed the hope that he might be long spared to use those abilities whica they all knew he possessed, in the higher sphere that he had reached. (Applause.) The Newton division he did not now represent, but, they might take it that he would still represent them in the Hon eof Lards. They had now to look for a successor, and be believed they had found the right mania Colonel Richard Pilkingtoe. (Cheers.) He was no stranger to them, no' carpet bagger ;" he had fought and worked alongside them year after year and they knew the work he had d one. He had an experience which very few gentlemen had hal ; ha had the municipal experience of a Mayor ; that of a volunteer as a commander, and as a oommerciat man he was an active partner in one of the largest concerns in this country. With such experience he thought they could rest assured that he would be a fit and proper representative lb- them to send to the House of Commons. (Applause.) He was certain Mr. Pilkiugton would represent them in an able and satisfac- tory manner and he heped they w_arld give him that welcome which an Earleetown audience generally gave to its representative. (Cheers.) Colonel Pilkingt en who had a most cordial reception, paid a tribute in his opening remarks to the work done by Lard Newton as the representative of the division. He proteeded t 3 say that he was a warm supporter and admirer of Lord Salisbury. He felt that the Adminis- tration of Lord Salisbury was one of the strongest, one of the best, one of the wisest Administrations that had taken charge of the affairs of the nation in this country. —(Oneers.) The Government had been in power for three and a half years. and much had been done in that time. How well everything had been done was shown by the condition of the trade of the country to-day. Month after month during the three and half years trad had gradually and steadily improved, There might. have been no great "boom" in trade, but, • better than that, progress had been continuous.—(Hear, hear.) In regard to home matters generally, he might say that many great measures had been passed, the crown of those measures being the conferring of county govern- ment on the three kingdoms. 'Twelve or thireen years ago Home Rule for Irelani was brought to the front. The Unionists of the country stayed the disin- tegration and disruption that were threatened, and the recent Local Government Bill foe Ireland had killed Home Rule altogether. (Hear, hear.) England, Seotland, Wales, and Ireland now had the best form of Home Rule for it came to them in the shape of clunty government. Besides the municipalities they had 113 county councas, and they had, ab we all these institu- tions, the Imperial Parliament—the grand, old, histaric Parliament.which could put any of those local autho- rites right should they do that which ,was witnout the law. The reconstruction of local government had been carried out on a thoroughly logical basis, and it consti- tuted one of the most beaefieent reforms of the century. (Cheers.) Then Lord Salisbury had put the army and navy in a thoroughly sound condition, so that this coun- try,a.nd. he believed, also the colonies, were now in a safe position. The fact gave firmness to the Govern- ment in matters of foreign policy. In Egypt Lord Salisbury had won his greatest suecess. A dozen years ago nobody would hive believed that Egypt could be placed in the position it was in to-day. What had been accomplished was the resu't of a steady,plodding policy; had been done by saying " We will never come out of Egypt "—because we never would come out of Eeypt. (Cheers.) Colonel Pilkington described the military eperations which had been carried on in Egypt and the successes achieved. The victory of Omdurman had,he said, wiped out a stain ea the honour of England. After the victory came the incident of Fashnda. Lord Kitchener, proceeding up the Nile found the French flag flaunting there, and a body of Frenchmen who appar- ently did not want to move. The idea seemed to be to gut in two our advance from Egypt to the Cape. But our Government stood firm' for it was a firm Government, and, moreover, it had behind it the great naval and nflitary forces to the building up and strengthening of which it had paid so much attention during the last few years. II" had also behind it a nation united almost to a man. The result was that the French Major left Fes- !axle as if he hai been simply an " em'ssary of civilisa- tion" and nothing more.—(Laughter and cheers.) Another great thing accomplished was the establishment of a warmer and better nndersteading with the United State3,—(Hear, hear.) E egla,nd, he believed, was the first of the five Great Powers of Europe. With America as her ally she might cheerfully face the troubles which were likely to arise in one or two quarters of the world. (Cheers,) Mr. R. Stone moved a resolution declaring Colonel Pilkington to be a fit and proper' person to represent the division in the House of Commons. The Liberals, he said, sieeme Ito he looking in vain for a candidate to oppose Colonel Piikington, and he did not think they would find the man. That did not mean that the Liberals were deficient in pluck, but that their better judgment would ',revel, to show to foreign Govern- ments the strength of the pitriotie feeling in this coun- try. Dr. Hendysirle seconded the resolution, which was suppoved by Captain Begot, M.P., and passed. Mr. T. D. Grimke Drayton moved a vote of thanks to Captain Begot. Mr. W. Catterall seconded and it was heartily carried. A similar compliment to the Chairman, terminated the proceedings.

div.head: FANCIERS' SHOVir AT NEWTON.
div.p: FANCIERS' SHOVir AT NEWTON.

On Sat ardai, the Newton-le-Willows Famiers' Asso- ciation h.,1,1 their firs.; annual all England Show of pout- try,..Vgeons, and cage birds in the Tewn Hill, Newton. There was a f tidy good response to the committee's in- vitation for entries. In tne poultry classes there were 244 entries, and in the pigeon class 116. There was not a numerous entry among the cage birds, and for this reason the committee had to cancel several of the classes. The Norwich, ticked, yellow or buff canaries, and the British birds hard and soft bills ware left in, and for these there were 33 entries, and the qualities were of a fair description. Amongst the poultry,the varieties of Indian game were of a verg good quality and amongst the Minorcas and Leghorns there was an excellent dis- play, the winners being strong all round. Tee Lang- sha.n or Oroingtons were rather po sr and amongst the Bantam Cocks there were a few very gooJ birds. There were some very useful birds included amongst the like- liest hens for laying purposes, and the drakes were of a good variety. In the "any variety cock" pigeon the white Trumpeter shown b 7 P. Pitchford was a noted winner and being in the pink of condition very easily gained first in that cl Ise, and special for best bird in the show. Amongst the flying homer cocks the competition was btrongly contested, several noted winners turning up. In the Members' Class fsr flying homer cock or hen the competition was very keen. There were some very fair birds, and several were competent to contest in the open clasFes. There was nothing very special about the cage birds, hut the canary shown by E. Simpson and Sons easily gained first and special for the best bird in the show. The judge for poultry and pigeons was Mr. P. Proud, Silverdale, and for cage birds, Mr. A. Wel- lings, Prescot. The birds were excellently staged, and the labours of the juige were in consequence very much lightened. The attendance of the general public was not numerous, but under all the circumstances, the tak- ings at the door were quite up to expectations. The New Yelr festival s3rvic3 wa3 held at Cairo- street Chapel, on Sunday evening, when a special ser- mon was preached by the R?v. W. H. Drummond to the younger member.; of the church. There was a good alendance of past and pressnt choir scholar 3, who had heel especially invited to attend, and the rev. gen.lP- mates sermon, which was full of interest, was much ap• preciat.d. MUSICAL SERVICE AT SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

This place of worship was completely filled on Sunday evening when a special musical service was held. Selec- tions from" The Messiah" were rendered by an aug- mented choir which was capably lead by Mr. Walter !Stough. Mr. E L'oyd Jones occupied the pulpit, and in the course ot his discourse he referred to some of the triumphs of Christianity, and to the work it had accom- plished in the church and the world. The soloists were Miss Hannah Brough (contralto); Mr. Arthur Griffiths (tenor); Mr. D. Fanshaw (bass). Mr. Arthur Griffiths was in good voice and gave an exceptionally fine render- ing of the recit and aria "Comfort ye" and " Every Valley." Miss H. Brough sang "Behold a Virgin,'' "0 Thou that tellest," and "He was despised;" her vocalisa- tion ot the latter aria being marked by cul- ture and pathos. Mr. D. Fanshaw's bass voice ! was heard to advantage in the recit " Thus saitla the Lord" and in the difficult and exacting arias "But who may abide" and "Why do the Nations?" The principal choruses in the oratorio including " And the Glory," "0 Thou that Tellest," "For unto us," "Be- hold the Lamb of God," " All we like sheep," "Lift up your heads," and " Hallelujah," were very credit- ably sung by the choir. Mr. T. Brough pre- sided at the organ and the accompaniments were rendered the more effective by the services of a small but efficient orchestral band of string and wind instruments. At the close a collection was taken on behalf of the choir funds, and realised a satis• laltory sum.

div.head: NOTES ON GVIE3 AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GVIE3 AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOO rtn.LL.

I feel inclined to apologise to nop r!a.ders f having led them to believe, bp a statement in this column a few weeks az°. that the Warrington team at the commence- meat of 1899 would be a " formidable combination." At that tune I had information which convinced me that the committee haa at last determined to secure out- side assistance for the team—if not at all costs at consi- derable sacrifice. Even now I believe theyihave made up their minds in this direction, but it is quite evident that coming to a right decision is not the onty thing required. Actioa—enterprising and decisive action—is absolutely necessary if players are to be persuaded to enrol then- selves under the Warrington banner: Only this last month the committee have been—and may be yet—in negotiation with a player who was described to me as a " real star." TLIDS3 negotiations have resulted in no- thing satisfactory, and now the Warrington F. C. Com- mittee are sitting illy at home waiting " to hear " from him. In all probability while they are waiting some agent with more enterprise and energy will have pounced upon him and got his signature on the pl.:nixed form of another club to whom " stars" of any magnitude are as welcome as to Warrington.

Advettlsing is one of the methods which the Warring- ton Football Ciub have resorted to in their endeavour to secure talent. I hava nothing to say against advertis- ing— far [run it—and the result of it has shown that there are more difficult ways of getting at the eltvidve footballer. Shoals of applications have Coale to War- rington from budding i iternationals whose knowledge of persuasive English was greater than their knowleige of Ruby football. H. Davies, the half-back who played with the" A" team on Saturday seams to have been one of these individuals. His recommendations were excellent, but it was soon seen that his football abilities were nil, and he has, it is rumoured, gone to seek fieldi and pastures new. Snould he find none harder than Warrington he will ba a lucky man. Adyertisin4 is a method which may be alright so far as securing appli- cations is c ,ncerned, but it does not facilitate the "signing on "of players worth haying. The committee or their representatives will have t 3 see for themselves. burry about somewhat, and not take things so easily ad round. lam quite willing t 3 give them credit for honest endeav(surs to strengthen the team,but those endeavours will have to be redoubled or nochiug will be gained, ani much time will be lost.

The Runcorn match—apart; from any others—lid a great deal towards showing what the Bt:elgth of the Warringeon team really amounts to. Runcorn have spent litt'e on 'heir team, but they are able to place a combination in the field superior to that at the command of the Warrington Committee. Tois fact ouzht to open the eyes of the men who govern the des`inies of the Warrington F.C. to the requisite extent. Men of some ability as footballers are not yet scarce, and they will have to be found, and when flund will have to be promptly secured. There is a way of being enterprising without being reckless, and other clubi in the Northern Union are demonstrating, this fact every week in the season.

It seems impossible for the Warrington men to win a match in the Manchester district. Satarcla.y was another case in point. The team journeyed to S Niaton with very poor prospects, and amongst; the players and everyone else in Warrington for that instter, the result was a foregone conclusion. The team was but of very moder- ate strength ; the play was also moderat ; and the re- sult was defeat by ten points to nil. Although beaten, the" primrose and blues " were not altogether dis- graced as was the case at Oldham. The f ,rwards played a stealing game,which was probably due to the fact that they were all playing for a position on tie team. It can hardly b 3 said that this constant changing of men —and there were five changes on Saturday—is a wise procedure. It tends to disorganise the team and makes combination diflioult if not imoessible.

There was an utter lack of method in t flew; and f ol- lowing up any advant ige gained against Swinton on Saturday. For aiearly the whole of the first half of the game Warrington were pressing severely. rho forwards heetel out fr3m the scrimmage and use.' their feet when the ball was in the oven, in a surprising manner. But still every effort to cross the line was easily checkmated; areater speed on the part of the home players largely accounting for this. There were even times when the termination of a pa3sing mvement found Lie Warring- ton players as far off the line as when they started. Then again some of the Warrington men need to p:tac- tise the art of goal-kicking. When a penalty kick does happen to be granted, the probability is that in nine eases out of ten nothing is gained by it. Warrington had a chance on Saturday to gi.A a couple of points in this manner, but the lack of areliable goal-kicker proved th 3 stumbling block.

Coming to the individual players the p'ale of honour must be given to Hallam. His play on Saturday was superb, and brat for his vigorous defensive work the Swinton score would have been muh larger. He returned the ball in a judicious manner, and put in some lofty points from touch. The only mistake he made was in following up a little too often, sometimes when it was apparent from the first that nothing could be gained by it. Bate was toe most unlucky player on the field. He wag not in great form but he gave the Swirstonians a fright on two occasions when near the line. The fates, however, seemed to have decreed that the Warringten team must bo nilled, and PO it was. The three-quarter line was extremely weak. None of the players dig- tinguishei themselves. Harris was placed hors de combat as the result of a foul charge by Worthington who left the marks of the s3los of his boots on Harris's body. Isherwood played his usual plucky game, but Cross and Moores were short of speed. The forwards to a man worked hard, and it would be invidious to pick out any for sw.cial

On the winning side was the only player to cross the Warrington lines and this he twice success- fully accomplished. In him the Swinton team have a decided acquisition and on Saturday's form a great deal will be heard of him. Valentine was as good as ever, and made the openings for Hampson. Messer and Lewis also played exceedingly well, and a better three-quarter line than that of Swinton's it would be difficult to get. Goodman has a predisposition to play to the gallery and it may cost him dear some day. In the half-back division Morgan and Pearson were a trifle superior to Batt and Ashurst, due to the former being more familiar with the ground. The Swinton forwards were beaten by the visitors but they did the best possible thing and that was to adopt determined defensive tactics which suc- ceeded in keep:ng Warrington out.

It will be seen that itaucoru nave at last climbed above Warrington in the table, and c3rrainlv their re- cord for the past few weeks has been an excellent one. Warrington are now in their usual place, the centre of the table, and will probably keep that unless there is a sudden acquisition of. strength. I hardiy fancy they will sink lower, though Rochdale Hornets are at present playing in very pro:nising form. This Saturday, War- rington journey to Wigan, and if they play with any- thing like determination they will win. The Wigan team is decidedly inferior to Warrington, except in the forward division where it holds an advantage. Last year Warrington were very unfortunate, and had a fair try disallowed. They ought to make no mistake on this occasion, and the two points are badly wanted.

Cross has been retained on the warn, and will partner Fish on the left wing. He is a reliable player, and per- haps the best of the three-quarters on the defence, but in attack he has been woeiully deficient this season. If he could only get back his speed he would be worth his place at any time. The forwards are a goad lot, and fairly weighty, and ought to hold their own with the Wigan eight if they work as they did at Swint)n.

The "A" team had a stiff encounter at Wilderspool on Saturday, but they emerged vict)rious though only Poorly representei. Swinton "A" had to bow the knee to Warrington "A" on their own heath, but they are a capable lot and were expected ta run Warrington 'closer than they did on Saturday. Duckworth, Ratcliffe,Allen and Nelson all played well on the attack, while Bascow was quite safe as a custodian.
The "A" team league re3ult3 up to dat3 are ai fallowe For.
Again st,

The Warrington Junior -League will select a team t 3 oppose the" A" team at Wilderspool to-day. They ought to be able to give the Warrington second string a good game, and may perhaps introduce one or two promising juniors. The " gate ' will help to keep the Junior League alive, and increase its usefulness, so that supporters of the game ought to attend in large numbers.

div.head: ALARUING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ALARUING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS.

A RAILWAY MAN'S PRESENCE OF MIND. An alarming accident, which caused a most ser- ious dislocation of traffic on the railway between Liverpool, St. Helens, and the North, occurred on the London and North-Western Railway, between St. Helens and Thatto Heath Stations on Monday night. Happily no personal injuries were sustained but more than one passenger train had an ex- tremely narrow escape from what might have proved an appalling disaster. During the afternoon and evening a hurricane of wind and rain passed over the St. Helens district, and one of its effects was the complete en.reofing of a shed on the premises of the Greengate Brick and Tile Company's Works, lying alongside the main line of the London and North-Western Railway, about 300 yards from Thatto Heath Station in the direction of St. Helens. About twenty yards of the• wooden roof of this shed was blown bodily over the fence of the works yard, and it toppled down the embankment of the deep railway cutting, fin- ally resting in an oblique direction across the rail- way lines. This occurred about twenty minutes to ! six—exactly a minute after the well-tilled passenger train leaving St. Helens at 535 p.m. for Prescot and Liverpool had passed the spot. Following the ' passenger train—about a couple of minutes later— was a ballast or goods train from St. Helens to Liverpool, and in the pitchy darkness the engine ran into the obstruction. The results were most alarming. The crashing of the timbers is described as having been terrific, while the powerfu! engine and teader left the rails and ploughed their way through tile wrecked roof as if it were matchwood. The engine and tender were! finally tappled over on their sides into the gutter !at the foet of the embankment. The driver of the ! engine, William Ralphe, of 10, High-street, Ince !Green, near Wigan, and the fireman, Arthur Burns, of Hall Farm, Hindley Green, naturally had very narrow escapes from serious injury or death. For- tunately, however, both men had the presence of mind to jump from their engine after striking the obstruction and leavino the rails, and they alighted in the four-foot a second or so before the locomotive toppled clean over. They were both badly shaken, and received several bruises. Three of the waggons following the engine were dragged from the-rails, while both lines were eempletely blocked with the d-molished roof. The brakesmen of the train, John Weston, of Liverpool, and his assistant, Azthur Bail y, also of Liverpool, immediately took steps to prevent any mishap to other trains, and to acquaint the officials with the setieas accident. Knowing that a passenger train from Liverpool to St. Helens was due to pass the spot at that moment, Bailey , stetted to run at full speed towards Thatto Heath Station, but stumbled over the wreckage, and his lamp was extinguished. He, however, continued. his journey, but whn about 200 yards from the station he noticed the passenger train approaching the scene of the accident. With commendable presence of mind he at once placed a couple of fog signals on the rails, and running forward shouted to the driver of the train, wits, after the explosion of the signals, pulled up the train just before the deeoerous spot was reached. The officials at Thatto Heath Station were afterwards informed, and messages were sent for help to St. Helens. Mr. Bo irdre en, stationmaster, and others at once proceeded to the spot, and for the/time being Mr. Boardman took charge of the arrangements for clearing the line. About an hour later a breakdown gang from St. Helens, under In- spector Whistlecroft, put in an appearance. In the meantime several passenger trains, both from Liver • - pool and St. Helens, were unable to pass the ob- struction, those from St Helens being sent on after some delay, round by St. Helens Junction. The line from Liverpool to St. Helens was sufficiently cleared to allow the trains to slowly pass the soot in the course of about two hours, but the clearance of the other line was a job which required many hours hard work. Arrangements were completed at late hour for the traffic to and from Liverpool to be worked on the single line system.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON DIVI- SION OF LANCASHIRE. IGENTLEM My representation of the Newton Division having now ceased I desire to express my deep and genuine regret at the severance of a connection which lasted uninterruptedly for twelve years. I desire also gratefully to acknowledge not only the confi- dence of my former constituents who three times returned Ille to Parliament by increasing majorities but also the con- sideration which I received from both supporters and oppon- ents. It will always be a satisfaction to me to tinnk that, in spite of hard fought contests, party Feeling iu the division has hitherto been practi, fly free from the bitterness which Is often manifested elsewhere. I need scarcely say that though ceasing to be your Member, I shall do my best to further your interests should opportunities occur, and I do not hesitate to add that who- ever may be my succcssor he will sit for a constituency which any man, however eminent, might consider it an honour to represent. NEWTON. December 31st, 1898.
